dishes.name: Doro Wat
steps: Start with the onions, since this is the base of the whole dish: finely chop 6 large red onions — you want small, even pieces, not big chunks. Put them in a dry pot (no oil yet) over medium heat.

Cook the onions completely dry, stirring every couple of minutes so they don't stick or burn. This takes 20-30 minutes and is not a step to rush — you're waiting for them to go from crunchy and white to soft, jammy, and deep golden-brown. If they start sticking badly, add a tiny splash of water, not oil.
Once the onions are soft and browned, add the niter kibbeh (spiced clarified butter) and stir it in. Let it melt and coat the onions for 2-3 minutes.

Add the berbere spice paste. Stir constantly for 3-5 minutes over medium-low heat — this 'blooms' the spices in the fat, which is what gives doro wat its deep flavor. The mixture will turn a darker brick-red and smell intensely fragrant. Don't walk away here; berbere can burn and turn bitter if left unstirred.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in a splash of water (about half a cup) to loosen the thick paste into a sauce, stirring to combine.

Add the chicken pieces and stir well so every piece is coated in the red sauce. Cover the pot and let it simmer on low heat for 45-60 minutes, stirring occasionally. You'll know it's ready when the chicken is fork-tender and the sauce has thickened to coat the back of a spoon.
Add the hard-boiled eggs whole, spooning some sauce over them so they soak up color and flavor. Let everything simmer together for a final 10 minutes.
Turn off the heat and stir in a squeeze of fresh lemon juice — this brightens the richness of the dish.
Serve hot, spooned over injera (or with injera on the side for scooping). Traditionally, everyone eats from the same platter, tearing off pieces of injera to scoop up the stew — no utensils needed.

dishes.name: Key Wat (Beef Stew)
steps: Finely chop the 4 large red onions. Heat a dry pot (no oil) over medium heat and cook the onions, stirring frequently, for 15-20 minutes until they turn soft, golden, and jammy - this slow cook is the foundation of the dish, so don't rush it.
Add 1/2 cup niter kibbeh to the softened onions and stir until melted and combined.
Add 3/4 cup berbere and cook, stirring constantly, for 3-5 minutes over medium-low heat, until deeply fragrant and darker in color - watch closely so it doesn't stick or burn.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, and cook for 2-3 minutes more.
Cut the beef into 1.5-inch cubes, add to the pot, and stir well to coat every piece in the sauce.

Pour in enough water to almost cover the meat (about 1.5-2 cups), bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 45-60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is very tender. Season with salt and serve hot with injera.

dishes.name: Sega Alicha (Mild Beef Stew)
steps: Cut the beef into 1 to 1.5-inch cubes.
Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent.
Add the minced garlic, minced ginger, and 1 teaspoon turmeric, and stir constantly for 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the beef cubes, stirring to coat them well in the onion-turmeric mixture, and cook for 3-4 minutes until the outside of the meat is no longer pink.

Pour in about 1/2 cup water, bring to a simmer, then cover and cook over low heat for 45-50 minutes, stirring occasionally and adding a splash more water if it looks dry, until the beef is fork-tender.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera or rice.

dishes.name: Doro Alicha (Mild Chicken Stew)
steps: Cut the chicken into serving pieces if not already done, and pat dry.
Heat 4 tablespoons niter kibbeh in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until very soft and translucent.
Add the minced garlic, minced ginger, and 1 teaspoon turmeric, and stir constantly for 1-2 minutes until fragrant and the onions turn golden.
Add the chicken pieces to the pot, turning them to coat well in the onion mixture, and cook for 3-4 minutes until the outside is no longer pink.
Pour in about 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 40 minutes, stirring occasionally and turning the chicken pieces, until fully cooked through and tender.
Add the peeled hard-boiled eggs, spooning some sauce over them, and simmer uncovered for 10 more minutes so they absorb flavor. Season with salt and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Tibs
steps: Cut the beef or lamb into 1-inch cubes and pat dry with a paper towel.
Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh (or oil) in a heavy pan over high heat until shimmering hot.
Add the meat cubes in a single layer, without crowding the pan, and sear for 2-3 minutes per side until well browned on the outside.
Add the sliced onion and rosemary sprig, and cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion softens.
Add the sliced peppers and diced tomato, and cook for another 5 minutes, stirring, until the vegetables soften slightly.
Stir in 1 tablespoon berbere if using, and cook for 2-3 more minutes. Remove the rosemary sprig, season with salt, and serve sizzling hot with injera or bread.

dishes.name: Zilzil Tibs (Strips of Beef)
steps: Slice the beef tenderloin thinly against the grain into long strips, about 1/4 inch thick.
Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh in a skillet over high heat until very hot and shimmering.

Add the beef strips in a single layer without overcrowding (work in batches if needed) and sear for about 1-2 minutes per side, until browned outside but still tender and pink in the middle - zilzil tibs is meant to be served on the rarer side, not well-done.
Add the sliced onion, rosemary sprig, and diced jalapeño to the pan, and cook for 3-5 minutes, stirring, until the onion softens slightly but still has some bite.
Remove the rosemary sprig.
Serve immediately while hot, traditionally with a small dish of mustard sauce on the side for dipping.

dishes.name: Gored Gored

ingredients.name: lean beef, cubed raw or lightly seared

steps: Cut the beef into small, even cubes, about 1/2 inch.
Warm the niter kibbeh gently in a small saucepan over low heat, just until melted (don't let it get hot enough to actually cook the meat if you're keeping this traditional and raw).
Pour the melted niter kibbeh over the raw beef cubes in a bowl and toss well so every piece is lightly coated.
If you prefer it lightly cooked rather than fully raw, quickly toss the coated cubes in a very hot pan for 30-60 seconds total, just to warm the outside without cooking through.
Transfer to a serving plate and sprinkle with mitmita or berbere.
Serve with a small bowl of awaze on the side for dipping.
ingredient_names: lean beef, cubed raw or lightly seared

dishes.name: Dulet
steps: Finely dice the tripe, liver, and lean beef into small, even pieces (or pulse briefly in a food processor if you prefer a finer texture) - keep the pieces small, roughly the size of rice grains.
Heat the niter kibbeh in a skillet over medium heat. Add the diced onion and diced jalapeño, and cook for 5 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the diced meats to the pan and cook over medium-high heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring frequently, until everything is browned and cooked through (the liver should no longer look pink or raw).
Stir in 1 tablespoon berbere, mixing well so it coats all the meat evenly.
Cook for another 4-5 minutes over medium heat, stirring often, until the mixture is well combined and slightly glossy from the fat.
Season with salt, taste, and adjust spice if needed. Serve hot with injera.

dishes.name: Kitfo
steps: Food safety first: kitfo is traditionally raw or barely warmed, so use only very fresh, high-quality lean beef from a trusted butcher, and keep it well chilled until you use it.
Trim the beef of any fat or sinew, then finely mince it by hand with a sharp knife (traditional method) or pulse it briefly in a food processor until finely ground but not pasty.
In a small saucepan, gently warm the niter kibbeh over low heat just until melted and liquid, then remove from heat and let it cool slightly so it's warm, not hot.
Place the minced beef in a mixing bowl, pour over the warm niter kibbeh, and add 2 tablespoons mitmita. Mix thoroughly with your hands or a spoon until every bit of meat is coated.
Stir in the koseret or basil if using, for extra fragrance.

Serve immediately at room temperature, mounded on a plate, with injera, ayib (fresh cheese), and cooked gomen on the side. If you'd rather not eat it raw, you can lightly cook it in a warm pan for 1-2 minutes, stirring, until just barely pink (this becomes closer to 'kitfo leb leb').

dishes.name: Kurt
steps: This dish is traditionally eaten completely raw, so food safety matters: use only very fresh, high-quality beef tenderloin bought the same day from a butcher you trust, and keep it chilled until you're ready to serve.
Trim off any visible fat, silver skin, or connective tissue from the tenderloin with a sharp knife.
Cut the meat into small, bite-sized cubes, about 1/2 to 3/4 inch. Keep your knife and cutting board very clean.
Arrange the cubes on a clean serving plate.
Put the awaze sauce and mustard into small separate bowls alongside the meat, so each person can dip their piece before eating.

Serve immediately - kurt is meant to be eaten fresh, right after cutting, not stored or reheated. If you're at all unsure about the meat's freshness, lightly searing the cubes in a hot dry pan for 30-60 seconds per side is a safer alternative, though it's no longer technically kurt.

dishes.name: Minchet Abish
steps: Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent.
Add 3 tablespoons berbere and the minced garlic, and stir constantly for 2-3 minutes over medium-low heat until fragrant and the mixture darkens slightly - don't let it burn.
Add the ground beef to the pot, breaking it up well with a spoon or spatula as it cooks, for 5-7 minutes until fully browned with no pink remaining.
Pour in a splash of water (about 1/2 cup) and bring to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook over low heat for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the flavors meld and the sauce thickens slightly.
Stir in 1 teaspoon abish (fenugreek) powder if using, during the last 2-3 minutes of cooking, for a subtle bitter-earthy depth.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot with injera.

dishes.name: Misir Wat
steps: Rinse 2 cups of red lentils in a fine strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. This removes excess starch and any debris.

Finely dice 2 medium red onions. In a pot, sauté them in a quarter cup of vegetable oil over medium heat until soft and translucent, about 8-10 minutes — stir occasionally so they cook evenly without browning too fast.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, and cook for 1-2 minutes until you can really smell them — that's your cue they're ready.
Stir in 3 tablespoons of berbere and 2 tablespoons of tomato paste. Cook this mixture for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens slightly and smells toasted rather than raw.
Add the rinsed lentils to the pot along with enough water to cover them by about an inch (roughly 3-4 cups). Stir well.

Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce the heat to a gentle simmer. Cover partially (leave the lid slightly ajar) and cook for 25-30 minutes, stirring every 5-8 minutes to prevent sticking on the bottom.

You'll know it's done when the lentils have completely broken down into a thick, spoonable stew — no individual grains should still be firm. If it looks too thick, add a splash more water; if too thin, simmer uncovered a bit longer.
Taste and add salt as needed — lentils absorb a lot of seasoning, so don't be shy.
Serve hot with injera or rice. This dish also reheats and freezes well, making it a great one to double.

dishes.name: Kik Alicha (Mild Split Pea Stew)
steps: Rinse 2 cups yellow split peas in a strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent (not browned).
Add the minced garlic and 1 teaspoon turmeric, and stir constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant - be careful not to let the garlic burn.
Add the rinsed split peas to the pot along with enough water to cover them by about an inch (roughly 4 cups).

Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover partially, and simmer for 25-30 minutes, stirring every so often so the peas don't stick to the bottom, until they're soft and starting to break down into a thick stew.
Season with salt to taste. If it's thicker than you like, stir in a splash more water. Serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Shiro Wat
steps: Finely dice 1 medium red onion. In a pot, heat 3 tablespoons of vegetable oil over medium heat and sauté the onion until soft and just starting to turn golden, about 5-7 minutes.
Add 2 minced garlic cloves and 1 diced tomato. Cook for 2-3 minutes until the tomato starts to break down and soften.
Pour in 3 cups of water and bring it to a gentle boil.

This next part matters: reduce the heat to low, then start whisking in the shiro powder gradually, a few spoonfuls at a time, whisking constantly. Adding it all at once will create lumps that are hard to smooth out.
Once all the shiro powder is incorporated, you'll have a thick, smooth, reddish-brown paste — about the texture of a loose hummus. Keep whisking or stirring every minute or so.
Simmer on low heat for 10-15 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't stick or scorch on the bottom of the pot. It will continue to thicken as it cooks.
If it gets too thick before the 10-15 minutes are up, stir in a little more warm water to loosen it back up.
Taste and adjust salt. It should taste rich, savory, and lightly spiced — not watery, and not stiff like paste.
Serve immediately while hot, with injera. Shiro thickens quickly as it cools, so this is a dish best eaten fresh off the stove.

dishes.name: Gomen (Collard Greens)
steps: Wash the collard greens thoroughly and chop them into thin ribbons, discarding any thick, tough stems.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the minced garlic, minced ginger, and diced jalapeño (if using), and stir for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped greens to the pot in batches if needed (they'll shrink down quickly), along with a splash of water. Stir to combine.
Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 15-20 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the greens are tender and dark green, but not mushy.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Atkilt Wat (Cabbage, Carrot & Potato)
steps: Peel and cube 3 medium potatoes, peel and slice 2 medium carrots, and thinly slice half a head of cabbage.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until soft.
Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric and cook for about 30 seconds until fragrant, turning the onions a bright golden color.
Add the cubed potato and sliced carrot along with a splash of water (about 1/4 cup). Cover and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the sliced cabbage on top, cover again, and cook for 10-15 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until all the vegetables are tender.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Fosolia (Green Beans & Carrots)
steps: Trim the ends off 1 lb green beans and cut them into 2-inch pieces. Peel and julienne (cut into thin matchsticks) 2 medium carrots.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until soft.
Add the julienned carrots and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they start to soften slightly.

Add the green beans along with a splash of water (about 1/4 cup). Cover the pot and cook over medium-low heat for 12-15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the beans are tender-crisp (cooked through but with a little bite left, not mushy).
Season with salt to taste.
Serve warm as a side dish, either on its own or alongside other stews.

dishes.name: Dinich Alicha (Potato Stew)
steps: Peel 4 medium potatoes and cut them into even 1-inch cubes so they cook at the same rate.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and translucent.
Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric and cook for about 30 seconds until fragrant - it will turn the onions a bright yellow.
Add the cubed potatoes and the diced jalapeño (if using), stirring to coat everything in the turmeric oil.

Pour in a splash of water (about 1/4 cup), cover the pot, and cook over medium-low heat for 18-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are fork-tender. Add a little more water if the pot looks dry.
Season with salt, stir gently (try not to mash the potatoes), and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Shimbra Asa (Chickpea "Fish")
steps: In a bowl, mix 1.5 cups chickpea flour with enough water (about 3/4 to 1 cup, added gradually) to form a stiff, workable dough, kneading briefly until smooth.
Divide the dough into small portions and shape each one into a flattened, elongated oval, loosely resembling a small fish - this is traditional but not essential to the taste.
Steam the patties over simmering water for about 12-15 minutes, or pan-fry them in a lightly oiled skillet for 3-4 minutes per side, until firm and cooked through (no longer doughy in the center).
Meanwhile, heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a separate pan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 tablespoon berbere and cook for 1-2 minutes until fragrant, then add a splash of water to form a light sauce.
Gently add the cooked patties to the sauce and simmer for 10 minutes, spooning sauce over them occasionally, until well coated and heated through. Serve with injera.

dishes.name: Azifa
steps: Rinse 1.5 cups green lentils under cold water, then place in a pot and cover with plenty of water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 20-25 minutes, checking often near the end, until the lentils are tender but still hold their shape (not mushy or falling apart).
Drain the lentils well and spread them on a plate or tray to cool to room temperature - this is important, as azifa is served cold or room temperature, not hot.
Once cooled, transfer the lentils to a bowl and mix in the minced red onion, minced jalapeño, 1 teaspoon mustard, 2 tablespoons lemon juice, and 2 tablespoons olive oil.
Season with salt to taste and stir everything together well.
Chill in the refrigerator for at least 20-30 minutes before serving as a cold salad, ideally with injera.

dishes.name: Timatim Salad
steps: Wash 3 medium tomatoes and cut each one into small, even dice (roughly 1/2-inch cubes). Put them in a mixing bowl.
Peel and finely dice 1 small onion. If raw onion tastes too sharp to you, rinse the diced onion briefly under cold water and pat dry - this softens the bite. Add it to the bowl with the tomatoes.
Slice the jalapeño in half lengthwise, scrape out the seeds and white ribs with a spoon if you want less heat, then finely dice it and add it to the bowl.
In a small cup, stir together 2 tablespoons lemon juice and 1 tablespoon olive oil with a pinch of salt.
Pour the dressing over the tomato mixture and toss gently with a spoon until everything is evenly coated.

Taste and add a little more salt or lemon juice if needed. Serve right away at room temperature, alongside injera or grilled meat - this salad is best fresh and shouldn't sit too long or the tomatoes will get watery.

dishes.name: Ful Medames
steps: Warm 2 cups cooked fava beans in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally.
Using the back of a spoon or a potato masher, lightly mash about half the beans right in the pan, leaving the rest whole - you want a chunky, not smooth, texture.
Dice 1 tomato, 1 small onion, and 1 jalapeño while the beans warm through.
Stir the diced tomato, onion, and jalapeño into the warm beans.
Add 2 tablespoons lemon juice and 2 tablespoons olive oil, stirring to combine.
Season generously with salt, taste, and adjust. Spoon into a serving bowl and serve warm with fresh bread for scooping.

dishes.name: Yataklete Kilkil (Mixed Vegetable Stew)
steps: Peel and cube 2 medium potatoes, peel and slice 2 medium carrots, and trim and cut 1 cup green beans into 2-inch pieces.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until soft.
Add the cubed potato and sliced carrot, along with a splash of water (about 1/4 cup). Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the green beans to the pot, cover again, and continue cooking for 10-12 more minutes, stirring every few minutes, until all the vegetables are tender when pierced with a fork.
If using, add the rosemary sprig for the last 5 minutes of cooking to infuse its flavor, then remove it before serving.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm, either as a side dish or a light meal with injera.

dishes.name: Tikil Gomen (Cabbage & Potato)
steps: Peel and cube 2 medium potatoes, and slice 1 medium carrot into rounds. Thinly slice half a head of cabbage.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 5 minutes until soft.
Stir in 1 teaspoon turmeric and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant and the onions turn golden yellow.
Add the cubed potato and sliced carrot, stir to coat in the turmeric oil, cover, and cook for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice.
Add the sliced cabbage on top, cover again, and cook for 10-15 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cabbage has wilted down and the potatoes and carrots are fork-tender.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Yebeg Wat (Lamb Stew)
steps: Cut the lamb into 1.5-inch cubes.

Finely chop the 3 large onions. Heat a dry pot over medium heat (no oil yet) and cook the onions, stirring frequently, for 15-20 minutes until they turn soft and golden - this slow start builds the base flavor.
Add the niter kibbeh and stir until melted and combined with the onions.
Add 1/2 cup berbere and cook, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until deeply fragrant and the mixture darkens.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, and cook for 1-2 minutes more.

Add the lamb cubes, stirring to coat in the sauce, then pour in enough water to almost cover the meat (about 1.5 cups). Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lamb is very tender. Season with salt and serve with injera.

dishes.name: Injera

teff flour: teff + all-purpose flour blend for faster ferment

steps: In a large bowl, whisk 4 cups of teff flour with 5 cups of water until you have a thin, smooth batter with no lumps — it should be about the consistency of heavy cream.

Cover the bowl loosely (a clean kitchen towel works well) and leave it at room temperature to ferment for 2-3 days. This is the step that gives injera its signature tangy flavor, so don't skip it or rush it. You'll know it's ready when it smells pleasantly sour, like sourdough, and has visible bubbles on the surface.
Once fermented, gently stir the batter — don't overmix, as you want to keep some of the airiness from fermentation.
Heat a large flat non-stick pan (a mitad if you have one, otherwise a large crepe pan or non-stick skillet works) over medium heat. Don't oil it — injera is traditionally cooked on a dry surface.

Once the pan is hot (a drop of batter should sizzle gently, not violently), pour the batter starting from the outside edge and spiraling inward to fill the pan in one continuous motion, similar to pouring a crepe.
Immediately cover the pan with a lid. Do not flip injera — it only cooks on one side.

Watch for small bubbles ('eyes') to form across the entire surface — this usually takes 2-3 minutes. The edges will start to lift away from the pan slightly and look dry, and the injera should no longer look wet or glossy on top.
Carefully lift the injera out using a flat spatula and lay it on a clean towel to cool. It should be spongy and slightly rubbery to the touch, with a honeycomb texture of tiny holes throughout.
Repeat with the remaining batter. Stack the cooked injera flat, covered with a towel, as you go — they'll stay soft and pliable this way.

If your first one or two don't turn out perfectly (too thick, tears when lifting, doesn't develop bubbles), that's completely normal — pan temperature usually needs a small adjustment. Lower the heat slightly if it's browning before bubbles form, or raise it slightly if it's taking more than 3-4 minutes.

dishes.name: Kita
steps: In a mixing bowl, combine 2 cups flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Make a well in the center and pour in 3/4 cup water and 1 tablespoon oil.

Mix with a spoon, then your hands, bringing everything together into a dough. Knead on a lightly floured surface for 5 minutes until it feels smooth and firm (add a little more flour if it's sticky, or a splash more water if it's too dry).
Cover the dough with a damp towel or plastic wrap and let it rest for 10 minutes - this relaxes the gluten and makes it easier to shape.
Turn the rested dough out and pat or press it into a flat, even round, about 1/2 inch thick and roughly the size of your pan.
Heat a dry (ungreased) griddle or heavy skillet over medium heat. Lay the flattened dough in the pan.

Cook for 5-8 minutes per side, flipping once, until both sides are golden-brown with some darker spots and the center is cooked through (press it lightly - it should spring back and not feel doughy). Slice and serve warm.

dishes.name: Ambasha
steps: In a small bowl, stir 1 teaspoon yeast and 2 tablespoons sugar into 1 cup warm water (it should feel like warm bathwater, not hot — hot water kills yeast). Let it sit undisturbed for 5-10 minutes until the surface gets foamy and bubbly. If nothing happens after 10 minutes, your yeast is dead — toss it and start over with fresh yeast, or the bread won't rise.
In a large mixing bowl, combine 3 cups flour and 1/2 teaspoon ground cardamom. Make a well in the center and pour in the foamy yeast mixture and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil.

Mix with a spoon until it becomes shaggy, then switch to your hands and knead right in the bowl or on a lightly floured counter for 8-10 minutes. You're kneading long enough when the dough turns from rough and sticky into a smooth, springy ball that bounces back slowly when you poke it.

Shape the dough into a ball, place it in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover with a damp towel or plastic wrap. Set it somewhere warm and draft-free for about 1 hour, until it has visibly doubled in size — press a finger into it, and if the dent stays instead of springing back, it's ready.
Punch the risen dough down gently to release the air, then shape it into a round, flat loaf about 1.5 inches thick on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper.

Using a sharp knife, score a shallow crosshatch or diamond pattern on top — this is traditional and also helps the loaf bake evenly. Cover loosely and let it rest another 15-20 minutes while your oven preheats.
Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F). Bake the loaf for 30-35 minutes, until the top is deep golden-brown and the loaf sounds hollow when you tap the bottom with your knuckle.

Let it cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes before slicing — cutting too early makes the inside gummy. Ambasha is slightly sweet and fragrant with cardamom; serve it in wedges, plain or with coffee.

dishes.name: Himbasha
steps: In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast and a spoonful of sugar in warm water. Let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy on top.

In a large bowl, combine the flour with the remaining sugar, cardamom, and a pinch of salt. Make a well in the center and pour in the yeast mixture along with melted butter and any additional milk or eggs the recipe calls for.
Mix and knead the dough for 8-10 minutes, either by hand on a floured surface or in a stand mixer, until smooth, soft, and elastic.
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp towel, and let rise in a warm place for about 1.5-2 hours, or until doubled in size.
Punch the dough down gently and shape it into a round loaf. Place it on a greased baking sheet or into a round pan, cover loosely, and let it rise again for 30-45 minutes.
Score a decorative crisscross or spiral pattern into the top of the loaf with a sharp knife — this is traditional and helps it bake evenly.
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30-35 minutes until deep golden-brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom.
Let cool on a wire rack for at least 15-20 minutes before slicing, as himbasha is traditionally served in wedges alongside coffee or tea for special occasions.

dishes.name: Dabo Kolo
steps: In a mixing bowl, whisk together 2 cups flour, 2 tablespoons sugar, a pinch of salt, and 1 teaspoon berbere or cumin if using, so the spice is evenly distributed before any liquid goes in.
Add 3 tablespoons vegetable oil and rub it into the flour with your fingers until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs — this is what gives dabo kolo its crunchy, short texture.

Slowly add 1/2 cup water, a little at a time, mixing with a fork or your hands after each addition. Stop adding water as soon as the mixture comes together into a firm, non-sticky dough — you may not need all of it. Knead briefly, just 1-2 minutes, until smooth.
Pinch off small pieces of dough and roll each one between your palms into a thin rope about the width of a pencil, roughly 6-8 inches long.
Cut each rope into small pellet-sized pieces, about 1/2 inch long, snipping with kitchen scissors or slicing with a knife. Spread them out on a baking sheet in a single layer, not touching.

Preheat your oven to 160°C (325°F). Bake for 20-25 minutes, stirring or shaking the pan every 7-8 minutes so they toast evenly on all sides, until deep golden-brown and firm all the way through — break one open to check it isn't doughy in the center.
Alternatively, toast them in a dry skillet over medium-low heat, stirring constantly for about 15-20 minutes, until golden and crisp.

Let the pieces cool completely on the pan before eating or storing — they crisp up further as they cool. Store in an airtight container; dabo kolo is a crunchy snack, traditionally nibbled alongside coffee.

dishes.name: Kolo (Roasted Barley & Nuts)
steps: Heat a dry, heavy-bottomed pan (no oil) over medium heat.

Add the barley and spread it out in an even layer. Stir constantly with a wooden spoon so it toasts evenly without burning - this takes about 10-12 minutes. You'll know it's ready when the grains turn golden-brown, smell nutty and toasted, and make a slight popping or crackling sound.
Transfer the toasted barley to a bowl. If using, toast the chickpeas and peanuts separately the same way (they may need less time, so watch them closely), then set aside.
Combine the toasted barley with the roasted chickpeas and peanuts, if using, in one large bowl.
Sprinkle with 1/2 teaspoon salt and toss to coat evenly.
Let cool completely before serving - kolo is eaten as a crunchy snack, often carried in a pocket or bag.

dishes.name: Sambusa

ingredients.name: thin dough wrappers or samosa wraps

steps: If using lentils, cook them first: simmer split lentils in water until soft, drain well, and season with salt and a spoonful of berbere. If using ground beef, brown it in a skillet over medium-high heat, breaking it up with a spoon, until no pink remains.

In the same pan (or a fresh one if you started with lentils), heat a little oil and sauté 1 finely diced small onion for 4-5 minutes until soft. Stir in 1 tablespoon berbere or minced jalapeño and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Combine the sautéed onion mixture with your cooked lentils or beef in a bowl. Taste and adjust salt and spice — this filling should taste bold on its own, since the wrapper is plain. Let the filling cool to room temperature before wrapping, or it will make the wrapper soggy.
Take one thin dough wrapper and cut it in half lengthwise to make two long rectangular strips (if using pre-made spring roll or samosa wrappers, they usually come as squares — cut those in half too).
Fold one corner of a strip over to form a small triangle pocket at one end. Spoon about 1 tablespoon of filling into the pocket.

Keep folding the triangle over itself, flag-style, all the way up the strip, keeping the folds snug so the filling stays sealed inside. Dab a little water on the final flap and press to seal the edge closed. Repeat with the remaining wrappers and filling.

Heat 2 cups vegetable oil in a deep, heavy pot to 350°F (175°C) — test by dropping in a small scrap of dough; it should sizzle and float within a couple seconds. Fry the sambusas in small batches (don't crowd the pot, or the oil temperature drops and they get greasy) for 2-3 minutes per side, until golden-brown and crisp.
Lift out with a slotted spoon onto a plate lined with paper towels to drain excess oil. Let them cool for a minute or two — the filling stays very hot — before serving.
ingredient_names: thin dough wrappers or samosa wraps

dishes.name: Genfo
steps: Bring 4 cups water to a rolling boil in a heavy-bottomed pot.
Reduce the heat to medium-low. While whisking constantly and vigorously with a whisk or sturdy spoon, gradually sprinkle in 2 cups flour, a little at a time, to prevent lumps from forming.
Keep stirring vigorously (it will take some arm strength) as the mixture thickens into a very stiff, heavy porridge, about 8-10 minutes total. It's ready when the spoon can stand up in it on its own.
Wet a large spoon with cold water and use it to scoop and shape the hot porridge into a smooth mound in a serving bowl. Use the back of the spoon to press a deep well into the center of the mound.
In a small pan, melt 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh and stir in 1 teaspoon berbere until combined.
Pour the spiced melted butter into the well in the center of the porridge. Serve warm, mixing the butter in gradually as you eat, working from the center outward.

dishes.name: Kinche
steps: Rinse 2 cups cracked wheat in a strainer under cold running water until the water runs clear.
Bring 4 cups water to a boil in a medium pot.
Add the rinsed cracked wheat and 1/2 teaspoon salt, and stir once.

Reduce the heat to low, cover partially, and simmer for 25-30 minutes, stirring every few minutes to prevent sticking or scorching on the bottom, until the wheat is soft and the mixture has thickened into a porridge.
Remove from heat and stir in 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh (or butter) until melted and fully incorporated.
Spoon into bowls and serve warm, often with a side of plain yogurt to spoon over the top.

dishes.name: Firfir (Injera Firfir)
steps: Tear the leftover injera into bite-sized pieces by hand and set aside.
Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh in a skillet over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, and cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft.
Add 2 tablespoons berbere and cook, stirring constantly, for 2-3 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in a splash of water (about 1/4 to 1/2 cup) to make a light, pourable sauce, stirring to combine.
Add the torn injera pieces to the pan, tossing gently with a spatula so every piece gets coated in the sauce.
Cook for another 2-3 minutes, stirring gently, until everything is warmed through and well combined - injera softens quickly, so don't overcook it into mush. Serve immediately, often for breakfast.

dishes.name: Chechebsa
steps: If making the flatbread from scratch, mix flour with water and a pinch of salt into a stiff dough, then cook it on a dry griddle over medium heat for about 4-5 minutes per side until cooked through and lightly browned. Let it cool slightly, then tear it by hand into bite-sized pieces.
In a small saucepan, melt 4 tablespoons niter kibbeh over low heat.
Stir in 1 tablespoon berbere and the minced garlic clove (if using), and cook for about 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant.
Add the torn flatbread pieces to the pan with the spiced butter.
Toss and stir gently for 2-3 minutes, until every piece is coated in the red, spiced butter and heated through.
Serve warm for breakfast, traditionally with a side of plain yogurt to balance the spice.

dishes.name: Ayib (Ethiopian Cottage Cheese)
steps: Pour fresh milk into a heavy-bottomed pot and warm it gently over low-medium heat, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching on the bottom.
Once the milk is warm (not boiling), stir in a splash of lemon juice or a spoonful of live yogurt as a starter culture, then remove from direct heat.
Let the mixture sit undisturbed in a warm spot for several hours, or overnight, until it separates into thick curds and thin, watery whey.
Once separated, gently warm the mixture again over low heat for a few minutes (without boiling) to help the curds firm up further and separate more cleanly from the whey.
Line a colander with cheesecloth or a clean thin towel and set it over a bowl. Pour in the curdled milk and let the whey drain through, gathering the cheesecloth up around the curds.
Let it drain for 30 minutes to a few hours, depending on how firm you want the final cheese — longer draining gives a firmer, drier ayib.
Transfer the soft, crumbly cheese to a bowl and season lightly with salt if desired. Serve fresh, often alongside spicy stews like gomen or as a cooling side to berbere-heavy dishes.

dishes.name: Besso (Roasted Barley Drink/Snack)
steps: If your barley flour isn't already roasted, toast it in a dry skillet over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon for 5-7 minutes, until it turns a light golden-brown and smells nutty and toasted. Watch closely, as flour can burn quickly. Let it cool before using.
Place the roasted barley flour in a bowl.
Gradually add the water or milk, a little at a time, stirring continuously with a spoon or whisk to avoid lumps.
Keep adding liquid and stirring until you reach your preferred consistency - use less liquid for a thick, moldable paste that can be eaten with your hands, or more liquid for a drinkable consistency.
Stir in sugar to taste, if using.
Serve immediately as a quick, energy-dense snack or drink.

dishes.name: Tere Sega (Raw Beef)

ingredients.name: very fresh beef tenderloin, sliced thin

steps: This dish is served completely raw, so start with only very fresh, high-quality beef tenderloin from a trusted butcher, kept cold until serving time.
Trim away any fat or connective tissue from the tenderloin.
Using a sharp knife, slice the meat as thinly as you can manage, cutting against the grain.
Arrange the thin slices attractively on a clean serving plate.
Serve immediately alongside small bowls of awaze or mustard for dipping.

If you're not confident about the meat's freshness or prefer not to eat raw beef, you can very quickly sear the slices in a hot pan for about 15-20 seconds per side - this isn't traditional but is a safer option.
ingredient_names: very fresh beef tenderloin, sliced thin

dishes.name: Zigni (Eritrean Beef Stew)
steps: Cut the beef into 1 to 1.5-inch cubes.
Finely chop the 3 large onions. Heat the niter kibbeh (or oil) in a pot over medium heat, add the onions, and cook for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and golden.
Add 1/2 cup berbere and 3 tablespoons tomato paste, and cook, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes until the mixture darkens and smells fragrant - don't let it stick or burn.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute more, then add the beef cubes, stirring well so every piece is coated in the sauce.
Pour in about 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is tender and the sauce has thickened.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot with injera or bread.

dishes.name: Tsebhi Derho (Eritrean Chicken Stew)
steps: Finely chop the 4 large onions. Heat a dry pot (no oil) over medium heat and cook the onions, stirring often, for 15-20 minutes until deeply softened and golden.
Add 4 tablespoons niter kibbeh, 1/2 cup berbere, and 2 tablespoons tomato paste, and cook, stirring constantly, for 3-5 minutes over medium-low heat, until fragrant and darker in color.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1-2 minutes more, then add the chicken pieces, turning to coat every piece thoroughly in the sauce.
Pour in about 1 cup water, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 45-50 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is fully cooked and tender.
Add the peeled hard-boiled eggs, spooning sauce over them, and simmer uncovered for 10 more minutes.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot with injera.

dishes.name: Hilbet (Eritrean Bean/Lentil Paste)
steps: Rinse the beans or lentils well, then place them in a pot with plenty of water — enough to cover by a couple of inches, since they'll absorb a lot as they cook.

Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook, partially covered, for 45-60 minutes (longer for whole beans, shorter for split lentils), stirring occasionally and adding more hot water if it gets too thick, until completely soft and starting to break down.

Once fully tender, mash the beans directly in the pot with a potato masher or the back of a large spoon, working them into a smooth, thick paste. For an extra-smooth texture, blend in batches in a food processor.

Return the paste to low heat and stir in a good pinch of salt and, if using, a spoonful of niter kibbeh for richness. Cook for another 5 minutes, stirring often, to concentrate the flavor and thicken it further — hilbet should be thick enough to hold a spoon standing up.
Spread the finished paste onto a serving plate in a smooth, even layer.
Serve warm or at room temperature with injera, as part of a fasting (vegan) platter alongside other stews.

dishes.name: Tihlo
steps: Place 2 cups roasted barley flour in a mixing bowl.

Add the hot water gradually, about a quarter cup at a time, mixing with a wooden spoon (and then your hands once it's cool enough to touch) after each addition, until you form a stiff, smooth dough that holds together without cracking.
Knead the dough briefly in the bowl for about 1 minute until it feels uniform.

Wet your hands with a little water (this keeps the dough from sticking) and pinch off small pieces, rolling each one between your palms into a smooth ball about the size of a large marble or small walnut.
Traditionally these balls are rolled and shaped using a special grooved wooden tool (also called a tihlo), but shaping them by hand into slightly flattened rounds works well too.
Serve the dumplings warm, alongside a bowl of hot, spicy berbere-based dipping sauce (a thin, meaty wat) - eat by dipping each dumpling into the sauce.

dishes.name: Asa Wat (Fish Stew)
steps: Cut the fish fillets into large chunks, about 2 inches, and pat dry with a paper towel.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent.
Add 3 tablespoons berbere, the minced garlic, and the diced tomato, and cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring often, until fragrant and the tomato breaks down.
Pour in about 1.5 cups water to make a sauce, stir well, and bring to a gentle simmer.

Carefully lower the fish pieces into the simmering sauce in a single layer. Cook gently, uncovered, for 10-12 minutes, spooning sauce over the fish occasionally, until it's just cooked through and flakes easily with a fork - avoid stirring roughly, as fish breaks apart easily.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Kai Sir (Beet Salad/Stew)
steps: Peel and cube 3 medium beets and 2 medium potatoes separately (keep them apart so the potatoes don't turn pink from the beet juice while boiling, unless you don't mind the color).
Boil the beets in a pot of salted water for 20-25 minutes, and the potatoes in a separate pot for 12-15 minutes, until both are fork-tender. Drain each and let cool slightly.
Meanwhile, heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a skillet over medium heat, add the diced onion, and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft. Add the diced jalapeño if using, and cook 1-2 more minutes.
In a large bowl, combine the cooked beets and potatoes with the sautéed onion.
Toss everything together gently with a spoon, being careful not to mash the vegetables too much.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm or at room temperature.

dishes.name: Kitfo Leb Leb (Lightly Cooked Kitfo)
steps: Use only very fresh, good-quality lean beef, finely minced by hand with a sharp knife or briefly pulsed in a food processor until finely ground but not pasty.
Warm the niter kibbeh in a skillet over low heat until melted and just starting to shimmer - keep the heat low, since the meat should only lightly cook, not fully cook through.
Add the minced beef and 2 tablespoons mitmita to the pan.

Stir gently and constantly with a spatula for 2-4 minutes over low heat. Watch the color of the meat closely: you're looking for it to turn from bright red to a light pink throughout, not brown or gray - this means it's 'leb leb' (lightly warmed), not fully cooked.
Remove from heat as soon as the color changes, since the meat will keep cooking a little in the residual heat of the pan.
Serve warm right away with injera, ayib, and gomen on the side.

dishes.name: Siljo
steps: In a pot, whisk 1 cup ground flaxseed and 2 tablespoons mustard powder into 3 cups water, whisking well to avoid clumps, until you have a smooth, slightly thick base.
Place the pot over medium heat and stir in 2 tablespoons berbere and the minced garlic.
Bring to a gentle simmer, stirring frequently, since ground flaxseed thickens quickly and can stick to the bottom of the pot.
Cook for 15-20 minutes, continuing to stir often, until the mixture has thickened into a smooth, slightly tangy, spicy sauce with the consistency of a thin gravy.
Taste and adjust salt and spice level as needed.
Pour into a serving bowl and serve as a tangy, spicy side dish alongside injera for dipping.

dishes.name: Marek (Eritrean Ground Beef & Egg Stew)
steps: Heat 3 tablespoons niter kibbeh (or oil) in a skillet over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 6-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft.
Add 2 tablespoons berbere and 1 tablespoon tomato paste, and cook, stirring constantly, for 2-3 minutes until fragrant and the mixture darkens slightly.
Add the ground beef, breaking it up well with a spoon, and cook for 6-8 minutes until fully browned with no pink remaining.
Pour in a splash of water (about 1/2 cup), bring to a simmer, and cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens slightly.
Using the back of a spoon, make 4 small wells in the meat mixture and crack an egg into each one.

Cover the pan and cook over low heat for 5-8 minutes, until the egg whites are set but the yolks are still slightly soft (or longer, if you prefer firm yolks). Serve hot directly from the pan with injera.

dishes.name: Birsen (Split Pea Puree)
steps: Rinse 2 cups yellow split peas and place them in a pot with enough water to cover by about 2 inches.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the peas are very soft and starting to fall apart.
Drain any excess water if needed, then blend the peas with an immersion blender, or mash thoroughly with a potato masher or fork, until you get a smooth, thick puree.

In a separate small pan, heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion, minced garlic, and 1/2 teaspoon cumin, and cook for 5-6 minutes, stirring, until the onion is soft and fragrant.
Stir the onion mixture into the pureed split peas, mixing well to combine.
Return the pot to low heat and simmer for another 3-5 minutes to bring the flavors together, stirring often since it can stick easily. Season with salt and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Dabo (Ethiopian Bread)
steps: In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast and a pinch of sugar in warm water, letting it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy.
In a large bowl, combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt. Make a well in the center and pour in the yeast mixture along with oil.

Mix and knead the dough for 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic, either by hand on a floured surface or with a stand mixer's dough hook — the dough should be soft but not sticky, so add a little more flour if needed.
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and let rise in a warm place for about 1.5-2 hours, until doubled in size.
Punch the dough down and shape it into a round loaf. Place it in a greased round pan or on a baking sheet, cover loosely, and let it rise again for 30-45 minutes.
Score the top with a shallow crisscross pattern using a sharp knife — this is traditional and helps the loaf bake evenly without cracking randomly.
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 35-40 minutes until deep golden-brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. Cover loosely with foil partway through if it's browning too fast.
Let cool on a wire rack for at least 20-30 minutes before slicing, as dabo is dense and needs time to set.

dishes.name: Mulmul
steps: In a small bowl, dissolve 1 teaspoon yeast and 2 tablespoons sugar in 1 cup warm water (it should feel warm to the touch but not hot, around 105-110°F/40-43°C - too hot will kill the yeast). Let it sit for 5-10 minutes until it looks foamy on top; if it doesn't foam, your yeast may be dead and you should start over with fresh yeast.
In a large bowl, combine 3 cups flour with the foamy yeast mixture and 2 tablespoons oil.
Mix, then knead the dough on a floured surface for about 8-10 minutes, until it becomes smooth, soft, and elastic (it should spring back slowly when poked).
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp towel or plastic wrap, and let it rise in a warm spot for 45-60 minutes, until roughly doubled in size.

Punch down the risen dough gently to release the air, then divide it into small, even pieces and shape each into a smooth round roll. Place them on a lined baking sheet, spaced apart, cover loosely, and let rise again for 15-20 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F). Bake the rolls for 25-30 minutes, until they're golden-brown on top and sound hollow when tapped on the bottom. Cool slightly before serving.

dishes.name: Kategna
steps: Melt the niter kibbeh in a small pan over low heat until fully liquid. Whisk in the berbere until you have a smooth, deep-red spiced butter paste.
Lay the injera pieces flat on a clean surface and spread the spiced butter generously and evenly over the entire surface, right to the edges.
Fold or roll the coated injera loosely, then place it on a dry, hot pan or griddle over medium heat.
Toast for 1-2 minutes per side, pressing gently, until the injera is warmed through and slightly crisp and blistered at the edges — watch closely since berbere butter can scorch quickly.
Remove from the heat, cut into wedges or strips, and serve warm, traditionally alongside a cup of Ethiopian coffee or tea.

dishes.name: Buna (Ethiopian Coffee)
steps: Rinse 1/2 cup green (unroasted) coffee beans in a sieve under cold water and shake off the excess water.
Heat a dry, heavy-bottomed pan (traditionally a flat pan called a mitad, but any skillet works) over medium heat. Add the beans in a single layer — no oil needed.

Roast the beans, stirring or shaking the pan constantly so they don't scorch, for about 10-15 minutes. They'll go from pale green to yellow to light brown to dark, glossy brown as the natural oils come to the surface — you're aiming for a medium-dark roast, similar to what you'd buy pre-roasted. You'll know they're close when you start to smell a strong, toasty coffee aroma and hear faint cracking sounds.

Remove the pan from heat immediately once the beans are dark and fragrant — they keep cooking from residual heat for a minute after you pull them, so don't wait until they look burnt. Let them cool for a few minutes.
Grind the cooled roasted beans into a fine-to-medium powder using a mortar and pestle (traditional) or a spice/coffee grinder, similar in texture to espresso grounds.
Bring 4 cups water to a boil in a jebena (traditional clay coffee pot) or a small saucepan. Add the ground coffee directly to the water.
Let it come back to a boil, then reduce the heat and let it simmer gently for about 5 minutes. Watch closely, as coffee grounds can foam up and boil over quickly.

Remove from heat and let the grounds settle to the bottom for a couple of minutes. Pour carefully into small cups, leaving the sediment behind in the pot, and serve with sugar to taste. Traditionally, buna is served in three rounds from the same grounds, each round slightly weaker than the last.

dishes.name: Tej (Honey Wine)
steps: Warm a portion of the water gently (not hot) and dissolve the honey into it thoroughly, stirring until fully combined — this makes it easier to mix evenly into the rest of the water.

Combine the honey-water mixture with the remaining water in a large, clean fermentation vessel (a glass jar or food-grade bucket works well), aiming for roughly a 1:2 to 1:3 ratio of honey to water depending on desired sweetness and strength.

If using gesho (hops-like flowering shrub) for fermentation, lightly toast the gesho leaves and stems, then add them to the honey-water mixture — this introduces the wild yeasts and bacteria needed for fermentation and gives tej its distinctive flavor.

Cover the vessel loosely (with a cloth or lid that allows gas to escape, not airtight) and let it sit at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, for 1-2 weeks, stirring occasionally, until it starts to bubble and smell fermented.

After the initial vigorous fermentation slows, strain out the gesho solids and transfer the liquid to a clean vessel to continue fermenting more quietly for another 1-2 weeks, or until it reaches the flavor and strength you like.
Taste periodically — tej can range from mildly sweet and lightly fizzy to strongly alcoholic and dry depending on how long it ferments.
Once it tastes right, strain again if needed and bottle it, refrigerating to slow further fermentation. Serve chilled in traditional berele glasses.

dishes.name: Shiro Fitfit
steps: Dice 1 small onion and mince 2 cloves garlic. Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a saucepan over medium heat, add the onion, and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant, then whisk in 3/4 cup shiro powder along with about 2 cups water, whisking constantly to avoid lumps.
Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer, stirring frequently (shiro sticks easily), and cook for 8-10 minutes until it thickens into a smooth, pourable sauce. Season with salt.
While the sauce simmers, tear the leftover injera into bite-sized pieces.
Add the torn injera to the pot of shiro sauce, stirring gently to coat every piece.
Cook for another 2-3 minutes, stirring, until the injera has softened and absorbed some of the sauce but still holds together. Serve warm, often for breakfast.

dishes.name: Denche (Boiled Corn & Beans)
steps: If using dried corn kernels and dried beans, place them in a large bowl, cover with plenty of cold water, and let them soak overnight (at least 8 hours) - they'll roughly double in size.
The next day, drain and rinse the soaked corn and beans, then put them in a large pot.
Cover with fresh water by about 2 inches and add 1 teaspoon salt.
Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a gentle simmer and partially cover the pot.
Cook for 35-40 minutes, checking occasionally and topping up with water if it runs low, until both the corn and beans are fully tender when you bite into one (not crunchy or chalky in the center).
Drain off any excess water and serve warm in a bowl as a simple snack, with extra salt on the side if you like.

dishes.name: Bamya Wat (Okra Stew)
steps: Wash the okra and slice it into rounds about 1/2 inch thick. If you've never cooked okra before: keep the pieces dry and don't stir it too much once it starts cooking, or it can turn slimy - a gentle touch keeps it pleasant.
Heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook for 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the minced garlic, diced tomato, and 1 tablespoon berbere. Cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring often, until the tomato breaks down and the mixture smells fragrant.
Add the sliced okra to the pot and stir gently just once or twice to combine.
Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 15-18 minutes, stirring only occasionally, until the okra is tender but still holds its shape.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm with injera.

dishes.name: Spaghetti Carbonara
dishes.description: Roman pasta dish with a creamy egg-and-cheese sauce, no cream used traditionally.
steps: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Salt it generously — it should taste like the sea. This is your only chance to season the pasta itself.

While the water heats, finely dice 6 oz of pancetta or guanciale. In a large, cold pan, add the pancetta and turn the heat to medium — starting it in a cold pan helps render the fat slowly without burning the meat. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until it's crisp and golden, with plenty of fat rendered into the pan. Turn off the heat but leave the pancetta and fat in the pan.

While the pancetta cooks, crack 4 whole eggs into a bowl and add 1 cup of finely grated pecorino romano and a generous amount of freshly cracked black pepper. Whisk together until smooth — this is your sauce, and it never touches direct heat, so mix it well now.

Cook 1 lb of spaghetti in the boiling water until al dente, about 1 minute less than the package says (it will finish cooking briefly in the pan). Before draining, scoop out at least 1 cup of the starchy pasta water and set it aside — you'll need this.
Drain the pasta and immediately add it to the pan with the pancetta (heat still off). Toss well so the noodles pick up the rendered fat.

Now, working quickly and off direct heat, pour the egg and cheese mixture over the hot pasta, tossing constantly and vigorously. The residual heat from the pasta and pan will gently cook the eggs into a silky sauce — not scrambled eggs. If it looks like it's clumping or scrambling, add a splash of the reserved pasta water and keep tossing; the starch helps keep everything smooth.
Keep adding small splashes of pasta water and tossing until the sauce coats every strand and looks glossy and creamy, not wet or dry.
Serve immediately in warmed bowls with extra grated pecorino and black pepper on top. Carbonara doesn't reheat well since the egg sauce can split, so this is a dish best made right before eating.

dishes.name: Pizza Margherita
dishes.description: Classic Neapolitan pizza topped simply with tomato, mozzarella, and basil.
steps: If your dough is cold from the fridge, let it come to room temperature for about 30 minutes first — cold dough is much harder to stretch and tends to spring back.

Preheat your oven as hot as it will go (ideally 500°F/260°C or higher) with a pizza stone or upside-down baking sheet inside, for at least 30 minutes before baking. A very hot oven is the single biggest factor in getting a good crust.

On a lightly floured surface, gently stretch the dough into a round using your fingertips, working from the center outward and leaving a slightly thicker border for the crust. Avoid using a rolling pin, which presses out the air bubbles you want.
Transfer the stretched dough to a floured pizza peel or the back of a baking sheet (this makes it easier to slide onto the hot stone).
Spread a thin, even layer of tomato sauce over the dough, leaving that border bare. Less is more here — too much sauce makes for a soggy crust.
Tear fresh mozzarella into small pieces by hand (rather than slicing) and scatter it evenly over the sauce.
Carefully slide the pizza onto the hot stone or baking sheet in the oven.

Bake for 8-12 minutes, watching closely rather than relying only on the timer — you're looking for the crust to be blistered and golden-brown in spots, and the cheese to be melted and just starting to brown.
Remove from the oven and immediately scatter fresh basil leaves and a drizzle of olive oil over the top — adding basil before baking would wilt and blacken it.
Let the pizza sit for 2-3 minutes before slicing; this helps the cheese set slightly so it doesn't slide off when you cut it.

dishes.name: Risotto alla Milanese
dishes.description: Creamy saffron-infused rice dish from Milan.
steps: Bring 4 cups chicken or vegetable stock to a gentle simmer in a saucepan and keep it warm on low heat next to your risotto pot the whole time you're cooking — adding cold stock shocks the rice and slows the cooking.
In a small bowl, crumble 1/2 teaspoon saffron threads and cover with a couple tablespoons of the warm stock to steep while you start the risotto — this draws out the color and flavor.
Melt 2 tablespoons of the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the minced small onion and cook for 4-5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not browned.

Add 1.5 cups arborio rice to the pan and stir constantly for 1-2 minutes — this is called toasting the rice, and you'll know it's done when the edges of the grains look slightly translucent while the center stays white.
Pour in 1/2 cup white wine and stir until it's fully absorbed and the raw alcohol smell is gone, about 1-2 minutes.

Now begin adding the warm stock one ladleful (about 1/2 cup) at a time, stirring frequently. Wait until each addition is almost fully absorbed before adding the next — this slow process is what makes risotto creamy, so don't rush it or dump it all in at once. This will take 18-22 minutes total.
About halfway through, stir in the saffron and its soaking liquid so the color develops evenly through the rice.

Keep tasting the rice as you go. It's done when the grains are tender but still have a slight bite in the center (al dente), and the risotto looks creamy and slightly loose — it should slowly spread out on a plate, not sit in a stiff mound.

Remove from heat and stir in the remaining 2 tablespoons butter and 1/2 cup grated parmesan vigorously — this final step, called mantecatura, is what gives risotto its glossy, luxurious texture. Season with salt to taste and serve immediately, since risotto stiffens as it cools.

dishes.name: Tacos al Pastor
dishes.description: Marinated, spit-roasted pork tacos with a touch of sweet pineapple.
steps: Toast 4 dried guajillo chiles briefly in a dry pan for about 30 seconds per side, just until fragrant and slightly pliable — don't let them blacken or they'll turn bitter. Remove the stems and seeds, then soak them in hot water for 15-20 minutes until soft.
Blend the softened chiles with achiote paste, a splash of pineapple juice, garlic, and a little vinegar until you have a smooth, thick, brick-red marinade.

Slice 2 lb of pork shoulder into thin steaks (about a quarter-inch thick). Coat the pork thoroughly in the marinade, making sure every piece is covered, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours — overnight gives the best flavor.
When ready to cook, heat a griddle or heavy skillet over high heat until very hot.

Cook the marinated pork slices in batches, without overcrowding the pan, for 2-3 minutes per side until the edges char slightly and the inside is cooked through. Don't move the pieces around too much while searing — let them sit so they actually develop that charred crust.
Once all the pork is cooked, chop it into small, bite-sized pieces on a cutting board.
In the same hot pan, quickly sear a few diced pineapple pieces for 1-2 minutes until lightly caramelized — optional but traditional, and adds sweetness against the smoky pork.
Warm your corn tortillas: the easiest way is directly over a gas flame for a few seconds per side, or in a dry skillet, until soft and slightly blistered, not stiff.
To assemble: stack two warm tortillas together (traditional, and helps prevent tearing), add a small pile of the chopped pork, a few pieces of seared pineapple, and top with diced onion and cilantro.
Serve immediately with lime wedges and salsa on the side.

dishes.name: Mole Poblano
dishes.description: Rich, complex sauce blending chiles and chocolate, served over chicken.
steps: Stem and seed 6 dried ancho and mulato chiles (wear gloves or wash your hands well after — the oils can sting your eyes). Toast them in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30-60 seconds per side, pressing down with a spatula, until they smell fragrant and become slightly pliable — don't let them blacken or they'll turn bitter.
Put the toasted chiles in a bowl and cover with hot water. Let them soak for 20 minutes until fully softened, then drain (reserve the soaking liquid).

While the chiles soak, season 2.5 lb chicken pieces with salt and brown them in a large pot with a little oil over medium-high heat, about 4-5 minutes per side, just to build flavor (they don't need to cook through yet). Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, char 2 tomatoes directly over the residual heat or under a broiler until the skins blister and blacken in spots, then roughly chop them.

In a blender, combine the drained soaked chiles, charred tomatoes, 1/4 cup almonds, and a cup of the reserved soaking liquid. Blend until completely smooth, adding more liquid as needed to help it move — this may take a couple of minutes and should end up the texture of a thick paste.

Pour the blended paste into the pot you browned the chicken in, straining it through a sieve if you want an extra-smooth sauce. Cook over medium heat, stirring often, for 8-10 minutes to deepen the flavor — it will sputter and pop, so use a splatter screen or lower the heat if needed.
Return the chicken to the pot, add enough water or stock to just cover it, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook over low heat for 35-40 minutes, until the chicken is fully cooked and tender.

Break 2 oz Mexican chocolate into pieces and stir it into the sauce during the last 5 minutes, letting it melt completely — this rounds out the bitterness of the chiles with a subtle sweetness. Taste and season with salt.
The sauce should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Serve the chicken smothered in mole, traditionally with rice and warm tortillas.

dishes.name: Chiles Rellenos
dishes.description: Stuffed, battered, and fried peppers in a light tomato sauce.
steps: Char 4 large poblano peppers directly over a gas flame, under a broiler, or on a hot grill, turning frequently, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over, about 8-10 minutes total.

Immediately place the charred peppers in a bowl and cover tightly with plastic wrap (or put them in a paper bag and fold it shut) for 10-15 minutes — the trapped steam loosens the skins so they slip off easily.

Once cool enough to handle, peel off the blackened skin under running water or by rubbing gently with a paper towel. Make a small slit down one side of each pepper and carefully remove the seeds and membranes with a spoon, keeping the pepper otherwise intact — this is delicate work, so go slowly to avoid tearing.
Stuff each pepper generously with shredded cheese (about 1.5 cups total), pressing the slit closed as best you can around the filling.

Separate 3 eggs. Beat the egg whites in a clean, dry bowl with an electric mixer until stiff peaks form (the mixture should hold its shape when you lift the beaters out). Gently fold in the egg yolks one at a time until just combined — don't overmix or you'll lose the fluffiness.
Dredge each stuffed pepper lightly in 1/4 cup flour, shaking off the excess, then dip it into the fluffy egg batter, coating it completely and thickly.

Heat 1 cup vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until hot but not smoking. Carefully lower each battered pepper into the oil and fry for 2-3 minutes per side, until the batter is puffed and golden-brown all over. Drain on paper towels.
Warm 2 cups tomato sauce in a saucepan while the peppers fry. Serve the fried peppers hot, topped or surrounded with the warm tomato sauce.

dishes.name: Butter Chicken (Murgh Makhani)
dishes.description: Creamy tomato-based curry, mild and rich.
steps: Cut 2 lb of boneless chicken thighs into bite-sized pieces. In a bowl, combine them with half a cup of yogurt, 2 tablespoons of garam masala, and minced ginger-garlic. Mix well so every piece is coated, cover, and marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour — overnight if you have time, for deeper flavor.

Heat a pan over medium-high heat (no oil needed if using a non-stick pan, or a small amount if not). Sear the marinated chicken in batches, not overcrowding the pan, for 2-3 minutes per side until charred at the edges and mostly cooked through. It doesn't need to be fully cooked yet — it'll finish in the sauce. Set aside.
In the same pan, melt 2 tablespoons of butter and sauté a diced onion until soft and lightly golden, about 5-6 minutes.
Add minced garlic and ginger, cooking for another minute until fragrant.
Pour in 2 cups of tomato puree and stir well. Let this simmer for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the raw tomato smell is gone and the sauce has thickened and deepened in color.
Using an immersion blender (or carefully transferring to a regular blender and back), blend the sauce until completely smooth — this step is what gives butter chicken its signature silky texture.
Return the sauce to the pan over low heat. Stir in the remaining butter and half a cup of cream, mixing until fully incorporated and glossy.
Add the seared chicken pieces back into the sauce, along with any juices that collected on the plate. Simmer gently for 10 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked and tender.
Taste and adjust — a pinch more garam masala, salt, or a touch of sugar if the tomatoes were too acidic.
Serve hot with basmati rice or naan, with an extra swirl of cream on top if you like.

dishes.name: Chana Masala
dishes.description: Spiced chickpea curry, a staple vegetarian dish.
steps: Finely dice 1 onion. Heat oil in a pan over medium heat and sauté the onion until soft and golden, about 6-8 minutes — don't rush this, as a well-cooked onion base is what gives the dish depth.
Add minced garlic and ginger, cooking for another minute until fragrant.

Add 2 diced tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they break down completely into a thick, jammy base — this takes about 8-10 minutes. You'll know it's ready when the oil starts to separate slightly at the edges of the mixture.
Stir in 2 tablespoons of garam masala along with cumin and coriander. Cook for 1-2 minutes, stirring constantly, to toast the spices in the fat and release their aroma.
Add the cooked (or canned, drained) chickpeas and stir well so they're coated in the spiced tomato base.
Pour in a splash of water — enough to loosen the mixture into a saucy consistency, not soupy — and bring to a simmer.

Let it simmer uncovered for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally. This gives the chickpeas time to soak up the flavor and lets the sauce thicken to your liking. Mash a few chickpeas against the side of the pan with your spoon partway through — this naturally thickens the sauce.
Finish with a good squeeze of lemon juice and fresh cilantro right before serving — this brightens the dish and balances the richness.
Serve hot with rice or warm naan.

dishes.name: Biryani
dishes.description: Layered, fragrant spiced rice dish, cooked with meat or vegetables.
steps: Marinate your chicken or lamb in yogurt, biryani masala, and a little ginger-garlic paste for at least an hour — this both flavors and tenderizes the meat.

Rinse the basmati rice under cold water until the water runs clear, then soak it in water for 20-30 minutes. This step matters: it helps the grains cook up long and separate instead of sticky and clumped.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Add the soaked, drained rice and cook it only about 70% of the way — it should still have a firm bite in the center when you taste a grain. Drain immediately and set aside; it will finish cooking later in step 6.
While the rice par-cooks, sear the marinated meat in a heavy-bottomed pot until browned on the outside, then set aside.
In the same pot, fry sliced onions until deeply golden and crisp — take your time here, as these fried onions are a key flavor and garnish layer, not just decoration.

Now build the layers: spread the seared meat in the bottom of the pot, then layer the partially-cooked rice on top. Scatter the fried onions, a drizzle of saffron dissolved in warm milk, and any fresh herbs (mint, cilantro) over the rice.
Cover the pot tightly — if your lid doesn't seal well, place a layer of foil underneath it to trap the steam completely.
Cook on very low heat for 20-25 minutes. This gentle steaming (called 'dum') finishes cooking the rice using the trapped steam and lets the flavors from the meat below rise up through the layers.
Turn off the heat and let it rest, still covered, for 5-10 minutes before opening — this helps everything settle.
To serve, gently fluff and mix from the bottom up with a wide spoon so you get a bit of meat, rice, and crispy onion in every scoop, rather than stirring hard and mashing the grains.

dishes.name: Dal Tadka
dishes.description: Simple, comforting lentil dish tempered with spiced ghee.
steps: Rinse yellow lentils (toor dal) under cold water until it runs mostly clear.
Simmer the lentils in water with a pinch of turmeric until fully soft and breaking down, about 20-25 minutes — you want them to lose their individual shape into a thick, spoonable consistency.
While they cook, prepare the tempering (tadka) separately: heat ghee in a small pan.

Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle a few seconds, then add minced garlic and a couple dried red chilies, cooking until the garlic is just golden — this only takes about a minute, so watch closely since garlic burns fast.
Pour the hot, sizzling tempering directly over the cooked lentils just before serving — this is added at the end, not cooked into the lentils from the start.
Stir it in and season with salt to taste.
Serve hot with rice or roti, with a lemon wedge on the side.

dishes.name: Kung Pao Chicken
dishes.description: Sichuan stir-fry balancing spicy, savory, and nutty flavors.
steps: Cut chicken breast into small, even cubes — about three-quarter inch pieces. Toss them with a little soy sauce and cornstarch and let them sit for 10-15 minutes; this quick marinade keeps the chicken tender and juicy through the high heat of stir-frying instead of turning tough.
Before you start cooking, have everything else prepped and within arm's reach — peanuts measured, dried chiles ready, sauce mixed. Stir-frying moves fast once it starts.
Mix the sauce ahead: combine soy sauce, a splash of rice vinegar, and a little sugar in a small bowl, and set aside.
Heat a wok or large skillet over high heat until it's genuinely hot — you should see a faint wisp of smoke from the oil, not just warm oil.

Add the marinated chicken and spread it out without stirring for the first 30-45 seconds — this lets it sear and brown rather than steam. Then stir-fry for another 2-3 minutes until just cooked through, and remove to a plate.

In the same hot wok, add a little more oil if needed, then add the dried chiles and Sichuan peppercorns. Stir constantly for about 30 seconds — just until fragrant, since they burn quickly and turn bitter if left too long.
Return the chicken to the wok along with the peanuts and the sauce mixture.
Toss everything together vigorously over high heat for about a minute, until the sauce reduces slightly and coats everything in a glossy layer.
Serve immediately over steamed rice while everything is still hot and the peanuts are still crunchy.

dishes.name: Mapo Tofu
dishes.description: Spicy, numbing tofu dish from Sichuan cuisine.
steps: Cut silken tofu into roughly one-inch cubes. Handle it gently, since it breaks apart easily — a wide spatula works better than tongs for moving it around later.
Heat oil in a wok over medium-high heat and add ground pork, breaking it into small crumbles as it browns, about 3-4 minutes.

Add doubanjiang (fermented chili bean paste) and minced garlic, stirring constantly for about a minute until the oil turns a deep red color and smells intensely savory — this color change is your cue the paste has released its flavor.
Add a splash of stock or water and bring it to a simmer.
Gently slide the tofu cubes into the sauce rather than stirring them in — stirring will just break them apart. Instead, tilt and shake the pan slightly to distribute the sauce around the tofu.
Let it simmer gently for about 5 minutes, spooning sauce over the top occasionally rather than stirring, so the tofu heats through without falling apart.
Mix a small amount of cornstarch with cold water to make a slurry, then pour it in, gently shaking the pan to distribute it evenly as the sauce thickens.
Once the sauce lightly coats the back of a spoon, finish with a sprinkle of ground Sichuan peppercorn and sliced scallion.
Serve immediately over steamed rice.

dishes.name: Dim Sum (Har Gow)
dishes.description: Steamed translucent dumplings filled with shrimp, a Cantonese classic.
steps: Make the dough first: in a heatproof bowl, whisk together 1 cup wheat starch and 1/4 cup tapioca starch. Pour in 1 cup boiling water all at once while stirring quickly with a wooden spoon or chopstick — the mixture will look shaggy and translucent.

As soon as it's cool enough to touch (careful, it's hot), knead the dough in the bowl for 3-4 minutes until it forms a smooth, slightly translucent, pliable ball. If it's too sticky, work in a little extra wheat starch. Cover with a damp cloth so it doesn't dry out.
Make the filling: combine 1 lb peeled, chopped shrimp with 1/4 cup minced bamboo shoots in a bowl. Season with a little salt, white pepper, and a small drizzle of sesame oil, and mix well.

Divide the dough into small pieces, about the size of a walnut, and keep the ones you're not using covered. Roll each piece into a ball, then flatten it with the flat side of an oiled knife or a small rolling pin into a very thin, round wrapper about 3 inches across — this dough is more fragile than regular flour dough, so press gently and evenly rather than rolling hard.

Place about 1 tablespoon of shrimp filling in the center of each wrapper. Fold the wrapper in half over the filling and pleat the edge, pressing firmly to seal — traditional har gow has 5-8 small pleats along the curved edge, but even simple pinched pleats work fine for holding it together.
Line a bamboo or metal steamer with parchment paper or lightly oiled cabbage leaves to prevent sticking. Arrange the dumplings inside, leaving space between each one since they'll expand slightly.
Bring water to a boil in a pot or wok, set the steamer on top, cover, and steam for 6-8 minutes, until the wrappers turn glossy and translucent and the shrimp filling is opaque and cooked through.
