Pound with a pestle using firm, repeated strokes — real physical effort, working separate chunks into one smooth, stretchy dough.
Fold the mass over itself periodically, wetting your pestle with a little reserved water to prevent sticking.
Keep pounding until completely smooth and elastic, stretching without breaking — this can take 15-20 minutes of steady work.
Shape into a smooth ball with wet hands.
Serve immediately, warm, with soup or stew for scooping.

dishes.name: Attiéké
dishes.description: Fermented, granulated cassava staple, similar in texture to couscous.
steps: Place the dried fermented cassava granules in a bowl and sprinkle the water evenly over them, a little at a time, tossing with your hands or a fork as you go so the moisture distributes evenly rather than pooling in one spot.
Let the moistened granules sit for 10-15 minutes, tossing once or twice, to fully absorb the water and soften slightly.
Transfer the granules to a steamer basket lined with cheesecloth, or a fine sieve set over a pot of simmering water, spreading them out in an even layer.
Steam, covered, for 15-20 minutes, until the granules are tender and translucent, fluffing with a fork halfway through to help them steam evenly and stay separate.
Remove from the steamer and fluff thoroughly with a fork, breaking up any clumps so the texture stays light and grainy, similar to couscous.
Serve warm alongside grilled fish, chicken, or vegetables, with a side of chopped tomato and onion or a spicy pepper sauce.

dishes.name: Kedjenou
dishes.description: Slow-simmered chicken stew cooked in a sealed clay pot for concentrated flavor.
steps: Combine chicken, tomato, onion, pepper, and ginger in a heavy pot with a tight-fitting lid.
Seal the pot tightly (traditionally with dough around the lid) to trap all the steam.
Cook over very low heat, shaking the pot occasionally instead of stirring, for about an hour.
Check that the chicken is fully tender before serving.
Serve with attieke or rice.

dishes.name: Groundnut Stew
dishes.description: Rich, nutty stew found across West Africa, built on a peanut paste base.
steps: Brown chicken or beef with diced onion in a large pot until good color develops.
Add chili pepper and cook another minute.
Stir in a generous amount of peanut butter, mixing until it coats everything.
Add crushed tomato and enough water to reach a stew consistency, stirring to fully dissolve the peanut butter.
Simmer, reduced to low heat, for 45 minutes to an hour, until the meat is tender.
Stir every 10 minutes or so, especially as it thickens later — peanut stews scorch more easily than plain tomato ones.
If it gets too thick before the meat is tender, thin with more water rather than letting it burn.
Taste and adjust — a pinch of sugar can balance a heavy peanut flavor.
Serve hot over rice or with fufu.

dishes.name: Akara
dishes.description: Deep-fried bean fritters, a popular Nigerian breakfast food.
steps: Soak black-eyed peas for a few hours or overnight, then rub them under running water to loosen and remove the skins — patient work, but the skins left in make the fritters heavier.
Blend the peeled peas with a little water, onion, and pepper into a thick, smooth batter.
Whip the batter vigorously by hand or with a mixer for several minutes — this aeration makes the fritters light rather than dense.
Test if enough air is whipped in by dropping a spoonful into a cup of water — if it floats, it's ready.
Heat oil for deep-frying until hot.
Drop spoonfuls into the oil, not overcrowding the pot.
Fry 3-4 minutes, turning occasionally, until deeply golden all over.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot, often for breakfast.

dishes.name: Efo Riro
dishes.description: Rich Yoruba vegetable soup made with leafy greens and palm oil.
steps: Sauté onion and blended pepper in palm oil until fragrant.
Add cooked assorted meat or fish and simmer briefly to absorb the flavors.
Add the leafy greens in batches, letting each wilt before adding more.
Simmer until the greens are tender but still vibrant, about 10 minutes.
Serve with pounded yam or rice.

dishes.name: Ndolé
dishes.description: Cameroon's national dish, combining bitter leaves with a nutty peanut sauce.
steps: If using fresh bitter leaves, wash and boil them multiple times, changing the water each time, to reduce bitterness — up to 3-4 rounds. Substitute spinach for a milder version if bitter leaves aren't available.
Blend or pound roasted, unsalted peanuts with a little water into a smooth paste.
Cook your chosen meat or fish until nearly done, then set aside.
Add the prepared bitter leaves (or spinach) and dried shrimp to the pot.
Stir in the peanut paste, mixing thoroughly with the greens.
Return the meat or fish with a little water to reach a thick stew consistency.
Simmer 20-30 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Taste and adjust with salt and pepper.
Serve hot with rice, plantain, or fufu.

dishes.name: Mafé
dishes.description: West African peanut stew, hearty and slightly sweet from the groundnut base.
steps: Brown beef chunks with diced onion until good color develops.
Stir in tomato paste, cooking 1-2 minutes until it darkens.
Add peanut butter and enough water to loosen into a sauce, stirring to fully incorporate.
Add sweet potato chunks.
Cover and simmer over low heat for about an hour, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching in the later, thicker stages.
Check the beef and sweet potato are tender; add more water if the sauce thickens too much before they're done.
Taste and adjust, adding chili for more heat if you like.
Serve hot over rice.

dishes.name: Nshima
dishes.description: Stiff maize porridge, Zambia's staple starch, eaten with relishes.
steps: Bring water to a boil.
Mix a portion of maize flour with cold water to make a paste, then stir it into the boiling water.
Cook, stirring, until it thickens.
Gradually add remaining flour, stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon until very stiff and smooth.
Shape into a mound and serve with vegetables or stew.

dishes.name: Sadza
dishes.description: Zimbabwe's staple maize porridge, similar to ugali and nshima.
steps: Bring water to a boil in a heavy pot.
Stir in a portion of maize flour to form a loose porridge, and cook a few minutes.
Gradually add the remaining flour, stirring constantly and vigorously.
Continue cooking and stirring until very thick and smooth, about 10 minutes.
Shape into a mound and serve with relish or stew.

dishes.name: Moambe Chicken
dishes.description: Chicken stewed in a rich palm nut sauce, widely considered a Congolese national dish.
steps: Brown chicken pieces with onion.
Add tomato and chili, cooking until softened.
Stir in palm nut cream (or palm oil with a little tomato paste as a substitute) and enough water to make a sauce.
Simmer until the chicken is tender and the sauce has thickened, about 40 minutes.
Serve with rice or fufu.

dishes.name: Matapa
dishes.description: Mozambican stew of cassava leaves cooked with ground peanuts and coconut milk.
steps: Wash and finely shred the cassava leaves (or substitute with finely chopped collard or spinach if cassava leaves aren't available) — traditionally they're pounded to break down the fibers.

Place the shredded leaves in a pot with a small amount of water and simmer, covered, over medium-low heat for 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they soften considerably and reduce in volume.
In a separate pan, sauté diced onion and garlic in a little oil until softened and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Add the sautéed onion and garlic to the pot of cooked leaves, along with ground peanuts (or peanut butter) and coconut milk, stirring to combine into a rich, thick sauce.
Simmer everything together for another 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and the flavors meld — add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
If adding shrimp or crab, stir it in during the last 5-8 minutes of cooking, just until cooked through.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot over rice or with xima (a cornmeal or cassava porridge).

dishes.name: Potjiekos
key_ingredients: slow-cooked in a cast iron pot
dishes.description: South African stew slow-cooked over coals in a three-legged cast iron pot.
steps: Brown meat in a cast iron pot over coals.
Layer onion, carrot, and potato on top of the meat without stirring.
Add stock, cover, and let cook slowly over low coals for several hours without stirring.
Check occasionally and add more liquid if needed.
Serve directly from the pot once the meat and vegetables are tender.

dishes.name: Vetkoek
dishes.description: South African fried dough bread, often stuffed with spiced mince or jam.
steps: In a small bowl, dissolve the sugar and yeast in the warm water (about 105-110°F/40-43°C — warm to the touch but not hot, or it will kill the yeast). Let it sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy on top; this tells you the yeast is active.

In a large bowl, combine the flour with a good pinch of salt. Pour in the foamy yeast mixture and mix until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead on a floured surface for about 5 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp cloth or plastic wrap, and let it rise in a warm spot for about an hour, or until doubled in size.
Punch the dough down gently to release the air, then divide it into 10-12 equal pieces. Roll each into a smooth ball and let them rest, covered, for 10-15 minutes.
Heat about 3 inches of oil in a deep, heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Test with a small piece of dough — it should sizzle and rise to the surface immediately.
Fry the dough balls in small batches (don't crowd the pot) for 4-6 minutes total, turning halfway, until puffed up and deep golden-brown all over. Drain on paper towels.
While still warm, split each vetkoek open with a knife (don't cut all the way through) and stuff generously with spiced mince filling or jam. Serve warm.

dishes.name: Matoke
dishes.description: Steamed and mashed green bananas, a staple across the African Great Lakes region.
steps: Peel green, unripe bananas carefully — starchy rather than sweet at this stage, closer to plantain.
Wrap the peeled bananas tightly in banana leaves or foil.
Place the wrapped bananas in a steamer or a pot with a small amount of water at the bottom, not touching the bundle.
Steam over low heat for about an hour, until completely soft when pressed.
Carefully unwrap — they should be very soft.
Mash directly in the wrapping or a bowl until smooth or slightly chunky.
Fold in a little sauce at this point if serving with a stew, or serve plain as a starchy side.
Serve warm alongside stews or grilled meats.

dishes.name: Luwombo
dishes.description: Ugandan stew steamed inside banana leaves for a distinct aroma.
steps: Prepare the meat (chicken, beef, or groundnut mixture) by cutting into pieces and seasoning with salt, pepper, and any spices you're using.
In a pot, sauté diced onion and tomato until softened and starting to break down, then add the seasoned meat and brown lightly on all sides.
If using a groundnut (peanut) sauce, stir in ground peanuts with a little water to form a smooth, thick sauce, and mix it into the meat along with any vegetables like mushrooms or okra.
Prepare banana leaves by passing them briefly over an open flame or dipping in hot water for a few seconds — this makes them pliable so they don't tear when folded.
Spoon the meat and sauce mixture into the center of a banana leaf, then fold the leaf up and around the filling, tying it securely with string or a strip of the leaf itself to make a sealed parcel.
Place the wrapped parcels in a large pot with a steamer rack, or directly in a small amount of simmering water, and steam for 1.5-2 hours, checking occasionally to keep water topped up.
Carefully unwrap the parcels at the table (the aroma is part of the experience) and serve the tender, richly flavored stew with matoke (steamed plantain) or rice.

dishes.name: Swahili Pilau
dishes.description: Fragrant spiced rice dish from the East African coast, influenced by Indian and Arab trade.
steps: Rinse the basmati rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear, then set aside to drain.
Heat oil or ghee in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add whole pilau spices (cardamom pods, cinnamon stick, cloves, cumin seeds) and toast for 30-60 seconds until fragrant.
Add sliced onion and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until deeply golden-brown — this caramelized onion is key to the dish's signature color and flavor, so don't rush it.
If using meat, add it now and brown on all sides, about 5-6 minutes.
Stir in minced garlic and ginger, cooking for another minute until fragrant, then add the drained rice, stirring to coat every grain in the spiced oil.
Pour in stock or water (about 1.5 times the volume of rice), season with salt, and bring to a boil.
Once boiling, reduce heat to the lowest setting, cover tightly, and cook undisturbed for 18-20 minutes until the rice is tender and all liquid is absorbed.
Remove from heat and let rest, covered, for 5-10 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork before serving, being careful not to break the grains.

dishes.name: Mandazi
dishes.description: Lightly sweet East African fried bread, similar to a doughnut.
steps: Dissolve yeast in a little warm coconut milk with a pinch of sugar, letting it foam 5-10 minutes.
Mix with flour, remaining coconut milk, sugar, and cardamom into a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Knead 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and let rise in a warm place about an hour, until doubled.
Punch down and roll to about a quarter-inch thickness.
Cut into triangles or diamonds.
Heat oil for frying to a moderate 325-350°F (160-175°C) — too hot and the outside browns before the inside cooks, since these are thick.
Fry in batches, turning occasionally, for about 3-4 minutes per side, until puffed and deeply golden.
Drain and cool slightly — delicious warm, like a lightly spiced doughnut.

dishes.name: Kachumbari
dishes.description: Fresh, tangy tomato and onion salad served alongside grilled meats.
steps: Dice 3 tomatoes and 1 onion into small, even pieces, roughly the same size so every bite has a mix.
Mince the chili finely, removing the seeds first if you want less heat.
Roughly chop 1/4 cup fresh cilantro.
In a mixing bowl, combine the diced tomato, onion, minced chili, and chopped cilantro.
Squeeze over 2 tablespoons fresh lime juice and season with salt to taste. Toss gently to combine.
Let it sit for 5-10 minutes before serving so the flavors meld, then serve fresh alongside grilled meats - it's best eaten the same day.

dishes.name: Hoppers (Appa)
dishes.description: Bowl-shaped fermented rice pancakes, often with an egg cooked in the center.
steps: Mix rice flour with a portion of coconut milk, a little sugar, and yeast into a thin, smooth batter, closer to crepe batter than pancake batter.
Cover and let ferment at room temperature a few hours, or overnight for more tang — this gives hoppers their characteristic slightly sour flavor and airy texture.
Just before cooking, stir in the remaining coconut milk to thin it slightly further.
Heat a small curved hopper pan (or small wok) over medium heat.
Pour a ladle of batter in and quickly swirl it around the sides with a wrist motion — this coats the sides thin while leaving batter pooled in the center, creating the bowl shape.
For egg hoppers, crack an egg into the center at this point.
Cover and cook 2-3 minutes, until edges are golden and crisp and the center is set.
Gently loosen the edges and lift out, keeping the bowl shape intact.
Serve immediately while warm, often with sambal or curry.

dishes.name: Kottu Roti
dishes.description: Sri Lankan street food of chopped roti stir-fried with vegetables and curry.
steps: Chop cooked flatbread into small strips.
Stir-fry mixed vegetables and egg on a hot flat griddle.
Add the chopped roti to the griddle along with curry sauce.
Toss and chop everything together vigorously using two flat blades (or spatulas), a signature technique.
Serve hot straight off the griddle.

dishes.name: Momo
dishes.description: Steamed or fried dumplings popular across Nepal and the Himalayas.
steps: Make a simple dough from flour and water, knead until smooth, cover and rest at least 20-30 minutes — this relaxes the gluten for easier rolling.
Mix ground meat or vegetable filling with minced onion, ginger, garlic, and seasoning, plus a splash of water or oil to keep it juicy.
Divide the rested dough into small balls and roll each into a thin round, slightly thinner at the edges.
Place a spoonful of filling in the center of each round.
Gather the edges up around the filling, pleating as you go, twisting to seal — takes practice, but even a simply pinched dumpling steams and tastes fine.
Arrange in a lightly oiled steamer basket, leaving space between them.
Steam over boiling water about 10-12 minutes, until the wrapper looks slightly translucent and filling is cooked through.
Serve hot with a spicy tomato-based dipping sauce (achar).

dishes.name: Dal Bhat
dishes.description: Nepal's everyday meal of lentil soup, rice, and vegetables.
steps: Rinse lentils, then simmer in water with a pinch of turmeric until soft and breaking down, about 20-25 minutes.
Prepare a tempering: heat ghee and sizzle cumin seeds and a dried red chili for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the sizzling tempering over the cooked lentils and stir in.
Separately, cook rice until fluffy.
Prepare a simple vegetable curry: sauté whatever vegetables you have with onion, garlic, and basic spices until tender.
Place rice in the center of a plate, with dal ladled generously alongside.
Add the vegetable curry in its own section, keeping components distinct.
Serve with a simple pickle (achar) if you have one for a sharp, tangy contrast.

dishes.name: Rogan Josh
dishes.description: Deep red, aromatic Kashmiri lamb curry.
steps: Brown lamb pieces in ghee, then set aside.
Sauté onion until deeply golden.
Add kashmiri chili and fennel powder, cooking until fragrant.
Return the lamb, stir in yogurt gradually to prevent curdling, then add water to cover.
Cover and simmer 1-1.5 hours until the lamb is tender and the sauce is deep red and thick.

dishes.name: Vindaloo
dishes.description: Fiery, tangy Goan curry with Portuguese roots.
steps: Blend vinegar, chilies, garlic, ginger, and mustard seeds into a smooth marinade paste.
Marinate the pork in this paste for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight.
Brown the marinated pork in a hot pot.
Add a little water and simmer covered for 1-1.5 hours until tender.
Uncover and reduce the sauce to the desired thickness before serving.

dishes.name: Dhokla
dishes.description: Steamed, spongy savory cake from Gujarat.

ingredients.name: eno fruit salt or baking soda

ingredient_names: eno fruit salt or baking soda
steps: Whisk chickpea flour with yogurt and water into a smooth, thick batter, then let it ferment or rest 20 minutes.
Stir in the eno or baking soda just before steaming, which activates and aerates the batter.
Pour into a greased pan and steam for 15-20 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.
Temper mustard seeds and curry leaves in hot oil, then pour over the steamed cake.
Cut into squares and serve with green chutney.

dishes.name: Pav Bhaji
dishes.description: Buttery mashed vegetable curry served with soft bread rolls, a Mumbai street food icon.
steps: Boil a mix of vegetables — potato, cauliflower, carrot, and peas — until very soft, almost falling apart. Slight overcooking here is actually correct, since this dish relies on a fully mashed texture.
Drain the vegetables well and mash them thoroughly, keeping just a little texture rather than a totally smooth puree.
In a separate pan, melt a generous amount of butter and sauté diced onion until soft.
Add diced tomato and pav bhaji masala, cooking until the tomato breaks down into a thick sauce.
Add the mashed vegetables and mix thoroughly, mashing further with your spoon as you stir.
Simmer for 10-15 minutes, adding a splash of water if it gets too thick, and mashing periodically — the more you mash and simmer, the smoother and more cohesive it becomes.
While it finishes, split pav bread rolls and toast on a griddle with plenty of butter until golden on both sides.
Finish the bhaji with a final pat of butter melted over the top just before serving.
Serve the hot bhaji with the buttery toasted rolls, diced onion, and a wedge of lime.

dishes.name: Chole Bhature
dishes.description: Spiced chickpeas served with fluffy deep-fried bread.
steps: Soak dried chickpeas overnight if starting from scratch, then simmer until fully tender — or use canned, well-drained chickpeas as a shortcut.
Sauté diced onion in oil until deeply golden, about 8-10 minutes — a well-browned base matters for the depth of flavor here.
Add diced tomato and cook until it breaks down completely into a thick, jammy sauce.
Stir in chole masala spice blend, cooking a minute or two until fragrant.
Add the cooked chickpeas with a splash of their cooking liquid, and simmer 15-20 minutes, mashing a few chickpeas against the pot's side to naturally thicken the sauce.

While that simmers, make the bhature dough: mix flour with yogurt and a little baking powder into a soft dough, then rest it for at least an hour — this rest is what makes the bread puff properly when fried.
Divide the rested dough into balls and roll each into an oval.
Heat oil for deep-frying until hot. Slide a dough piece in and gently press and splash hot oil over the top — this encourages it to puff into a big air pocket.
Fry until golden on both sides, about 1-2 minutes total, then drain.
Serve the hot, puffy bhature alongside the spiced chickpeas.

dishes.name: Idli Sambar
dishes.description: Soft steamed rice cakes served with a tangy lentil stew, a South Indian breakfast staple.

ingredients.name: idli rice and urad dal batter

ingredient_names: idli rice and urad dal batter
steps: Pour fermented idli batter into greased molds and steam for 10-12 minutes until fluffy.
Meanwhile, cook toor dal until soft and mash it.
Sauté vegetables, then add tamarind paste, sambar powder, and the cooked dal with water to make a stew.
Simmer until the vegetables are tender.
Serve the steamed idli with hot sambar and coconut chutney.

dishes.name: Aloo Gobi
dishes.description: Simple, popular dry-spiced potato and cauliflower dish.
steps: Cut potato and cauliflower into similarly sized pieces so they cook at roughly the same rate.
Heat oil and add cumin seeds, letting them sizzle a few seconds until fragrant — this is fast, so don't walk away.
Add minced ginger and cook another 30 seconds.
Add the potato and cauliflower along with turmeric, stirring well so everything is coated in the yellow spice.
Cover and cook over medium-low heat, stirring every few minutes, for about 15-20 minutes — covering steams the vegetables through evenly rather than just frying the outside.
Check doneness by piercing a potato piece — it should go in easily but the vegetables should still hold their shape.
If it's getting dry or sticking before fully tender, add a small splash of water and continue cooking covered.
Finish with fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lemon.
Serve hot as a side with rice, dal, or roti.

dishes.name: Chow Mein
dishes.description: Crispy or soft stir-fried noodles with vegetables and often meat.
steps: If using dried noodles, cook according to package directions until just tender, then rinse under cold water and toss with a little oil while you prep everything else.
Slice your protein and vegetables into thin, even pieces — uniform sizes cook more evenly in the short time this dish spends in the wok.
Heat a wok over high heat until genuinely hot.
Add oil, then your protein, stir-frying until just cooked through, then remove to a plate.
Stir-fry the harder vegetables first, then add softer ones a minute or so later, so everything finishes tender-crisp at the same time.
Push the vegetables to one side and add the noodles directly to the hot, empty part of the pan — letting them touch the hot surface directly gives a little char and smoky flavor.
Return the protein to the pan and add soy sauce, tossing everything together vigorously over high heat for a minute or two.
Serve immediately while hot and the vegetables still have some crunch.

dishes.name: Congee
dishes.description: Comforting rice porridge, eaten across East Asia with savory toppings.
steps: Rinse rice well under cold water.
Combine the rice with plenty of water or stock — roughly 6-8 times the volume of rice, since the goal is a loose, porridge-like consistency.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer.
Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally at first and more often as it thickens, for 1 to 1.5 hours.
This is a slow process — the rice gradually breaks down and the liquid thickens over this time, so no need to rush with higher heat, which risks scorching.
Add more water during cooking if it's getting too thick too soon.
Once smooth and creamy with no distinct grains left, season with salt.
Ladle into bowls and top with sliced scallion, a soft-boiled or century egg, shredded chicken, or crispy fried shallots.
Serve hot, freshly made.

dishes.name: Jiaozi (Chinese Dumplings)
dishes.description: Boiled, steamed, or pan-fried dumplings, essential to Lunar New Year meals.
steps: In a bowl, mix 1 lb of ground pork with finely minced cabbage, scallion, ginger, and a couple tablespoons of soy sauce. Stir the mixture in one direction (not back and forth) for a minute or two — this helps develop a better texture so the filling binds together instead of crumbling apart when cooked.
Lay a dumpling wrapper flat in your palm. Keep the rest covered with a damp towel while you work, since they dry out and crack quickly if left exposed.
Spoon about a teaspoon of filling into the center — don't overfill, or it'll be hard to seal and may burst while cooking.
Dip your finger in water and run it along the edge of half the wrapper — this acts as glue.

Fold the wrapper in half over the filling into a half-moon shape, pinching the center closed first. Then, working from the center outward, make small pleats along one side while pressing it against the flat other side, sealing as you go. Don't worry if your first few look rough — the pleating takes practice, and even imperfect dumplings taste great.
Place finished dumplings on a lightly floured tray without letting them touch (they'll stick together otherwise).
To boil: drop dumplings into boiling water. When they float, add a splash of cold water and let it return to a boil — repeat once more, then they're done.

To pan-fry: heat oil in a pan, arrange dumplings flat-side down, cook until the bottoms are golden (about 2 minutes), then add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam for 5-6 minutes. Uncover and let the bottoms crisp for another minute.
Serve with a dipping sauce of soy sauce, rice vinegar, and a little chili oil.

dishes.name: Spring Rolls
dishes.description: Crispy fried rolls filled with vegetables or meat.
steps: Stir-fry shredded cabbage, carrot, and mushroom until just softened, then let cool.
Place a spoonful of the vegetable filling on each wrapper.
Roll tightly, folding in the sides, and seal the edge with a little water or flour paste.
Deep fry until golden and crisp.
Serve with a sweet chili or soy dipping sauce.

dishes.name: Buuz
dishes.description: Mongolian steamed meat dumplings, traditionally eaten during Lunar New Year.
steps: Make a simple dough from flour and water, knead until smooth, cover and rest 20-30 minutes.
Mix ground mutton or beef with minced onion and a little water to keep the filling moist.
Divide the rested dough into small balls and roll each into a thin round.
Place a spoonful of filling in the center of each round.
Gather the edges up around the filling, pleating around the circumference, and twist to seal at the top.
Arrange in a steamer, leaving space between each so they don't stick.
Steam over boiling water about 15-20 minutes, until fully cooked.
Serve hot, traditionally eaten by hand — bite a small opening first to release the hot juices before eating the rest.

dishes.name: Khorkhog
dishes.description: Mongolian barbecue where meat is cooked with hot stones in a sealed pot.

ingredients.name: hot stones (or a heavy sealed pot)

ingredient_names: hot stones (or a heavy sealed pot)
steps: Heat stones over an open fire until very hot (or heat a heavy sealed pot as a substitute).
Layer meat, vegetables, and hot stones alternately in a large sealed vessel.
Seal tightly and cook over the fire, shaking occasionally, until the meat is very tender, about 1.5-2 hours.
Open carefully, as steam will be intense.
Serve the meat and vegetables together, traditionally passing the warm stones as a hand-warmer.

dishes.name: Taiwanese Beef Noodle Soup
dishes.description: Rich, soy-braised beef broth over hand-pulled noodles.
steps: Braise beef shank in soy sauce, star anise, and aromatics until very tender, about 2 hours.
Strain the braising liquid to use as the soup base, adding more stock as needed.
Cook wheat noodles separately until tender.
Slice the braised beef.
Assemble bowls with noodles, broth, sliced beef, and scallion.

dishes.name: Gua Bao
dishes.description: Fluffy steamed bun folded around braised pork belly.
steps: Braise pork belly slowly in soy sauce, sugar, and aromatics until completely tender and easily pulled apart with a fork, about 1.5-2 hours of gentle simmering.
Prepare or steam bao buns according to package directions, or make dough from scratch.
Steam the buns until puffy and fully cooked, about 10-12 minutes.
Once the pork is tender, remove and rest briefly, then slice into finger-thick pieces.
Open a steamed bao bun gently along its fold.
Tuck a slice or two of braised pork inside.
Add a spoonful of pickled mustard greens for tang and crunch.
Finish with crushed peanuts.
Serve immediately while the bun is still warm.

dishes.name: Hong Kong Egg Tart
dishes.description: Hong Kong's take on the Portuguese egg tart, with a lighter custard.
steps: If making pastry from scratch, prepare a flaky or shortcrust dough and chill well before rolling.
Roll thin and line small tart tins, pressing gently into the corners without stretching.
Chill the lined shells at least 15-20 minutes before filling — helps prevent shrinking or slumping during baking.
Whisk eggs with sugar and evaporated milk, being careful not to whip in too many bubbles.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve — this small step gives the signature ultra-smooth, glassy custard surface.
Carefully pour the strained custard into the chilled shells, filling nearly to the top.
Bake at 400°F (200°C) for about 10 minutes to set the pastry, then reduce to 325°F (165°C) for another 12-15 minutes, until just set with a slight jiggle.
Avoid opening the oven door too often — sudden temperature changes can crack or bubble the custard unevenly.
Let cool slightly before removing from the tins; best enjoyed slightly warm or at room temperature.

dishes.name: Fish Amok
dishes.description: Cambodia's national dish: fish steamed in coconut curry inside a banana leaf.
steps: Blend the kroeung spice paste (lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, garlic, shallot) until smooth — blending it fresh yourself works fine if pre-made isn't available.
Whisk the paste together with coconut milk and a beaten egg to create a light, custard-like base.
Cut fish into bite-sized chunks and gently fold into the coconut mixture.
Fold and pin banana leaves into small cup shapes to hold the mixture (a small heatproof bowl works as a substitute).
Spoon the fish mixture into the cups or bowls.
Place into a steamer, making sure the water doesn't touch them directly.
Steam about 20-25 minutes, until the custard has set firm, like a savory flan, and the fish is fully cooked.
Check by gently shaking a cup — it should hold together, not look liquid.
Serve warm, topped with a little extra coconut cream and shredded kaffir lime leaf.

dishes.name: Lok Lak
dishes.description: Stir-fried marinated beef cubes served over salad with a tangy dipping sauce.
steps: Marinate beef cubes in garlic, soy sauce, and a little sugar for 20 minutes.
Sear the beef quickly in a very hot pan or wok until browned but still tender.
Toss with oyster sauce just before removing from heat.
Serve over a bed of lettuce and sliced tomato.
Serve with lime pepper dipping sauce on the side.

dishes.name: Larb
dishes.description: Spicy, herby minced meat salad, considered Laos' national dish.
steps: Toast raw rice grains in a dry pan, stirring frequently, until deep golden-brown and distinctly nutty-smelling.
Grind the toasted rice into a coarse powder using a mortar and pestle — texture, not fine powder, so pulse briefly.
Cook ground pork or chicken in a dry pan, breaking into small crumbles, until just cooked — no oil needed.
Remove from heat and immediately toss the hot meat with fish sauce and plenty of fresh lime juice.
Stir in the toasted rice powder for its nutty flavor and characteristic texture.
Fold in torn mint, chopped cilantro, and thinly sliced shallot.
Taste and adjust — larb should taste vibrantly sour, salty, and a little spicy.
Serve at room temperature with sticky rice and cabbage or lettuce for scooping.

dishes.name: Mohinga
dishes.description: Myanmar's beloved breakfast fish noodle soup.
steps: Simmer a whole fish with lemongrass, ginger, and aromatics until fully cooked, then remove the bones and flake the meat, reserving the poaching liquid as broth.
In a separate pot, sauté sliced onion and garlic until softened.
Add the flaked fish back in with banana stem (or hearts of palm as a substitute).
Pour in the reserved liquid, plus more water or stock if needed.
Simmer 15-20 minutes to let flavors meld.
Whisk a little chickpea flour with cold water until smooth, then stir into the soup — this thickens the broth to a light, silky consistency.
Cook rice noodles separately.
Divide noodles into bowls and ladle the hot broth over them.
Top with crispy fritters, a hard-boiled egg, and cilantro.
Serve immediately, often for breakfast.

dishes.name: Tea Leaf Salad
dishes.description: Distinctive Burmese salad built on fermented tea leaves.
steps: If using raw tea leaves, blanch them briefly in hot water, then let them ferment/pickle for several days to weeks before use (many cooks use store-bought fermented tea leaf paste to skip this step).
In a small bowl, mix the fermented tea leaves with minced garlic, a splash of oil, and a squeeze of lime juice, mashing slightly to combine into a fragrant, tangy paste.

Toast the dried beans and seeds separately (split peas, peanuts, sesame seeds) in a dry pan over medium heat for 3-5 minutes each, stirring often, until golden and fragrant — toast them separately since they cook at different rates.
Thinly slice tomatoes and set aside. Roughly chop cabbage if using, or leave it as a bed for the salad.
In a large bowl, combine the tea leaf paste with the toasted nuts and seeds, sliced tomatoes, and shredded cabbage.
Dress with a little more oil, a squeeze of lime juice, and a pinch of salt, then toss everything together thoroughly right before serving so the crunchy elements don't go soft.
Serve immediately, mixing again at the table for the best combination of textures.

dishes.name: Nasi Lemak
dishes.description: Malaysia's national dish: fragrant coconut rice with spicy sambal and sides.
steps: Rinse rice well, then cook it with coconut milk instead of plain water, along with a pandan leaf if you have one, for extra fragrance.

While the rice cooks, make the sambal: blend dried chilies, shallot, and shrimp paste into a paste, then fry it in oil over medium heat, stirring often, for 10-15 minutes until deeply reduced, dark red, and glossy — this slow frying develops sambal's intense flavor, so don't rush it.
Season the sambal with a little sugar and salt to balance the heat.
Fry small dried anchovies in a separate pan until crisp, then drain.
Fry peanuts in the same oil until golden, then drain.
Boil eggs to preference and slice them in half.
Once the coconut rice is done, fluff it with a fork.
To plate: scoop the rice onto a plate, add a spoonful of sambal on the side, and arrange the fried anchovies, peanuts, boiled egg, and cucumber slices around it.
Serve at room temperature or slightly warm, which is traditional.

dishes.name: Char Kway Teow
dishes.description: Smoky wok-fried flat noodles, a hawker classic.

ingredients.name: soy sauce and dark soy sauce

ingredient_names: soy sauce and dark soy sauce
steps: Have everything prepped and within reach before cooking — this dish moves fast once it hits the wok.
Heat a wok over the highest heat your stove has until genuinely smoking hot — this dish's signature smoky flavor depends on intense heat.
Add oil, then shrimp, stir-frying about a minute until they start turning pink, then push to one side.
Crack an egg into the empty space and scramble quickly, then mix with the shrimp.
Add flat rice noodles along with soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and a little sugar.
Toss everything together vigorously and continuously, letting the noodles touch the hot wok surface directly for brief moments to pick up char.
Fold in bean sprouts right at the end, tossing just until barely wilted — adding them too early makes them soggy.
The whole process from noodles to finished should take only 2-3 minutes of constant tossing.
Serve immediately while hot and smoky.

dishes.name: Roti Canai
dishes.description: Flaky, layered flatbread griddled fresh, usually served with curry.
steps: Mix flour with water, a little condensed milk, and a pinch of salt into a soft dough. Knead until smooth.
Rub the dough generously with oil all over, then cover and rest at least an hour — this relaxes the gluten enough to stretch paper-thin later.
Divide into balls, coat each in more oil, and rest another 15-20 minutes.

On an oiled surface, flatten a dough ball, then gently stretch and flip it, working from the center outward until nearly translucent — this takes practice, and it's normal for a first attempt to tear a little.
Fold the stretched dough over itself into a loose square or coil, tucking edges under — this creates the flaky layers.
Heat a flat griddle with a little ghee over medium heat.
Flatten the folded dough gently and place on the hot griddle.
Cook 2-3 minutes per side, pressing occasionally, until golden with visible flaky layers.
Clap the roti briefly between your hands to separate and fluff the internal layers.
Serve warm with dhal or curry for dipping.

dishes.name: Pancit
dishes.description: Filipino noodle dish traditionally served at birthdays for long life.
steps: Soak rice noodles in warm water until pliable, about 15-20 minutes, then drain well.
Stir-fry sliced chicken until browned and cooked through, then remove and set aside.
Stir-fry shrimp briefly until just pink, then remove and set aside as well.
Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant, then add mixed vegetables, stir-frying until just tender-crisp.
Push the vegetables aside and add the soaked noodles along with soy sauce and a splash of broth.
Toss everything together, letting the noodles absorb the liquid — add more broth if they look dry.
Return the chicken and shrimp and toss to combine.
Taste and adjust seasoning with more soy sauce if needed.
Serve hot — traditionally at celebrations, where the long noodles symbolize long life, so it's customary not to cut them before serving.

dishes.name: Sinigang
dishes.description: Sour tamarind-based Filipino soup, a comfort food staple.
steps: Simmer pork or shrimp with sliced onion and tomato until the pork is becoming tender, about 30-40 minutes, or just a few minutes for shrimp.
Add tamarind soup base or fresh tamarind pulp — taste and adjust for a pleasantly tangy, not overwhelming, sourness.
Add radish and firmer vegetables first, simmering until they begin to soften.
Add water spinach or other leafy greens near the very end, wilting for just a minute or two.
Season with fish sauce.
Taste and adjust sourness and saltiness — it should be tangy and savory together, not flat.
Serve hot with steamed rice, ladling the soup generously over each bowl.

dishes.name: Lechon
dishes.description: Whole spit-roasted pig with crackling skin, centerpiece of Filipino celebrations.
steps: Stuff the cavity of the pig with lemongrass and garlic.
Season the skin generously with salt.
Skewer the pig on a large rotisserie spit.
Roast slowly over charcoal for several hours, turning constantly, until the skin is deeply crackling and the meat is tender.
Carve and serve with a liver-based dipping sauce.

dishes.name: Halo-Halo
dishes.description: Layered shaved ice dessert loaded with sweet toppings and ube ice cream.
steps: Gather your mix-ins in small bowls: sweetened red beans, kaong (sugar palm fruit), nata de coco, sweetened banana or jackfruit, and any other candied fruits or jellies you're using.
In a tall glass, layer a generous spoonful of each sweet mix-in on the bottom, one at a time, so you build up layers of different colors and textures.
Fill the glass most of the way with finely shaved or crushed ice, packing it in gently.
Pour evaporated milk (or a mix of evaporated and condensed milk) over the ice — pour slowly around the edges so it seeps down through the layers rather than just sitting on top.
Top with a scoop of ube halaya (purple yam jam) and a scoop of leche flan if using — these traditionally sit proudly on top rather than mixed in.
Serve immediately with a long spoon, and tell whoever's eating it to mix everything together from the bottom up before the first bite — 'halo-halo' literally means 'mix-mix.'

dishes.name: Gỏi Cuốn (Fresh Spring Rolls)
dishes.description: Fresh, unfried rice paper rolls filled with herbs, shrimp, and noodles.
steps: Cook the rice vermicelli according to the package instructions (usually a brief boil or soak in hot water for a few minutes), then drain and rinse under cold water to stop the cooking and prevent sticking. Set aside.

Fill a wide, shallow dish with warm (not hot) water. Working with one rice paper wrapper at a time, dip it into the water for about 10-15 seconds, just until it starts to soften - it will continue softening after you remove it, so don't over-soak it or it will tear.

Lay the softened wrapper flat on a clean, damp cutting board or plate. Near the bottom third of the wrapper, layer a small handful of lettuce and herbs, a small portion of vermicelli, and 2-3 pieces of cooked shrimp arranged in a neat row (shrimp cut-side up if halved looks nicer through the wrapper).
Fold the bottom edge of the wrapper up and over the filling, then fold in the left and right sides snugly.
Continue rolling upward tightly, like a burrito, keeping steady, gentle pressure so the roll stays compact but doesn't tear.
Repeat with the remaining wrappers and filling. Serve fresh, cut in half if desired, with peanut dipping sauce.

dishes.name: Khao Soi
dishes.description: Northern Thai curry noodle soup topped with crispy fried noodles.
steps: Fry the khao soi curry paste in a spoonful of thick coconut cream (skimmed off an unshaken can) over medium heat for a few minutes until deeply fragrant.
Add chicken pieces and stir to coat them in the fried paste.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and bring to a gentle simmer.
Let it simmer for 15-20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and tender.
While the curry simmers, cook fresh egg noodles, then divide most of them (saving a small handful) into serving bowls.
Fry that reserved handful of noodles in hot oil until crisp and golden — this crunchy topping is a signature contrast, so don't skip it.
Ladle the hot curry broth and chicken over the noodles.
Top with the crispy fried noodles, pickled mustard greens, sliced shallot, and a wedge of lime.
Serve immediately, encouraging everyone to squeeze lime and mix in the crispy noodles before eating.

dishes.name: Meat Pie
dishes.description: Individual-sized savory pie filled with minced meat and gravy, an Australian icon.
steps: Brown ground beef with diced onion.
Stir in gravy and simmer until thick and rich.
Let the filling cool, then spoon into pastry-lined individual pie tins.
Top with another layer of pastry, sealing the edges and venting the top.
Bake at 400°F (200°C) until the pastry is puffed and golden, about 25 minutes.

dishes.name: Pavlova
dishes.description: Crisp-shelled, marshmallowy meringue dessert topped with fruit and cream.
steps: Whip egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually add sugar, whipping to stiff, glossy peaks.
Fold in cornstarch and vinegar gently.
Shape the meringue into a large round on a lined baking sheet, building up the sides slightly.
Bake at a low temperature (250°F/120°C) for about 1.5 hours, then let cool completely in the oven.
Top with whipped cream and fresh fruit just before serving.

dishes.name: Vegemite on Toast
dishes.description: Simple Australian breakfast built on the famously polarizing yeast spread.
steps: Toast 2 slices of bread in a toaster or under a broiler until golden-brown and crisp.
While the toast is still hot, spread 1 tablespoon butter evenly over each slice so it melts slightly into the bread.

Scoop a very small amount of vegemite - about 1/4 teaspoon per slice to start - onto the buttered toast. Vegemite is intensely salty and concentrated, so less is genuinely more, especially the first time you try it.

Using the back of a knife or spoon, spread the vegemite as thinly as possible, working it out toward the edges in a light, even layer - you should barely be able to see it, not a thick spread like jam.
If it tastes too strong, you can always add a touch more; it's much easier to add more than to fix an over-spread slice.
Cut in half if desired and serve immediately while the toast is still warm.

dishes.name: Hāngī
dishes.description: Māori method of cooking food in a pit oven with heated stones.
steps: Heat stones in a large pit fire until glowing hot.
Wrap meats and vegetables separately in leaves or foil.
Place the wrapped food over the hot stones in the pit.
Cover everything with earth or a heavy covering to trap the steam completely.
Let cook undisturbed for 3-4 hours, then carefully uncover and serve.

dishes.name: Poke
dishes.description: Diced raw fish salad, a Hawaiian staple now popular worldwide.
steps: Use only very fresh, sushi-grade or otherwise trustworthy raw tuna. Cut it into even, bite-sized cubes, about 1/2 to 3/4 inch, using a sharp knife with clean, single cutting motions rather than sawing back and forth.
Place the cubed tuna in a mixing bowl.
Pour in 1/4 cup soy sauce and 2 tablespoons sesame oil, and add the chopped scallion.
Gently toss everything together with a spoon, being careful not to break up the fish cubes too much.
If adding other mix-ins like seaweed, diced onion, or crushed macadamia nuts, fold them in now.
Cover and let the mixture marinate in the refrigerator for 10-15 minutes to absorb the flavors, then serve chilled over rice or on its own.

dishes.name: Kalua Pig
dishes.description: Whole pig slow-roasted in an underground imu oven, a luau centerpiece.
steps: Rub the pork generously with sea salt.
Wrap tightly in banana leaves.
Traditionally, bury with hot stones in an underground pit (imu); alternatively, slow roast at 275°F (135°C) wrapped tightly.
Cook low and slow for 6-8 hours until completely tender.
Shred the meat and serve with its juices.

dishes.name: Pabellón Criollo
dishes.description: Venezuela's national dish combining shredded beef, beans, rice, and plantain.
steps: Simmer beef until very tender, then shred it and simmer briefly in a light tomato sauce.
Cook black beans with onion and garlic until flavorful.
Cook white rice separately.
Fry sliced ripe plantain until caramelized.
Plate the rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantain together in separate sections.

dishes.name: Cachapa
dishes.description: Sweet corn pancake, often folded around soft cheese.
steps: Blend fresh corn kernels with a little cornmeal and sugar into a thick batter.
Cook ladlefuls on a hot griddle like a pancake until set and lightly golden.
Flip and cook the other side.
Fold a slice of soft cheese into the warm cachapa.
Serve immediately while warm and the cheese is melting.

dishes.name: Bandeja Paisa
dishes.description: Massive Colombian platter combining beans, rice, meats, and egg.
steps: Cook the red beans with a piece of pork (if using) in plenty of water over low heat for 1.5-2 hours, or until very tender and the liquid has thickened into a flavorful sauce; season with salt.
Cook the rice separately according to package instructions, using a 2:1 water-to-rice ratio, until fluffy and fully tender.

Heat a skillet over medium-high heat and grill or pan-fry the chorizo links for 8-10 minutes, turning occasionally, until browned and cooked through. In the same or a separate pan, season the ground beef and cook, breaking it up, for 6-8 minutes until fully browned.
Fry the eggs sunny-side up in a lightly oiled pan for 2-3 minutes, until the whites are set and yolks are still soft.
Slice the avocado.
Arrange the rice, beans, chorizo, ground beef, fried egg, and avocado all together on one large platter, traditionally alongside fried plantain and arepa, so everyone can mix and match bites.

dishes.name: Ajiaco
dishes.description: Bogotá's hearty chicken and potato soup, made with a native Andean herb.

ingredients.name: corn on the cob, cut into pieces

ingredient_names: corn on the cob, cut into pieces
steps: Simmer chicken in a large pot of water with onion and garlic until tender.
Remove chicken, shred it, and set aside.
Add all three types of potato to the broth, cooking until some break down to thicken the soup while others hold their shape.
Add corn and guasca herb, simmering until the corn is tender.
Return shredded chicken to the pot and serve with capers and cream on the side.

dishes.name: Llapingachos
dishes.description: Cheese-stuffed potato patties, a staple of Ecuadorian cuisine.
steps: Boil 4 large potatoes in salted water until very tender, about 15-20 minutes, then drain well and mash thoroughly while still warm (a few small lumps are fine).
Mix 2 tablespoons achiote oil into the mashed potato until it's evenly colored a warm orange-yellow and well combined.
Fold in 1 cup shredded cheese, mixing until evenly distributed throughout the potato mixture. Season with salt.
Divide the mixture into equal portions and shape each into a flat, round patty about 1/2 inch thick, pressing firmly so they hold together (wetting your hands slightly helps prevent sticking).

Heat a lightly oiled griddle or skillet over medium heat. Cook the patties for 4-5 minutes per side, pressing gently once, until golden-brown and crisp on the outside, with the cheese inside slightly melted.
Serve hot with peanut sauce, and traditionally alongside a fried egg and a simple salad.

dishes.name: Encebollado
dishes.description: Ecuadorian fish and cassava soup, popular as a hangover cure.
steps: Simmer fish in water with onion and tomato until just cooked, then flake it.
Cook yuca chunks in the same broth until very tender.
Combine the flaked fish and yuca back into the broth.
Top generously with pickled red onion.
Serve hot with lime and popcorn or plantain chips on the side, as is traditional.

dishes.name: Salteñas
dishes.description: Bolivian baked empanada-like pastry filled with juicy, slightly sweet stew.

ingredients.name: beef or chicken stew, thick and slightly sweet

ingredient_names: beef or chicken stew, thick and slightly sweet
steps: Make a stew filling that's thicker and slightly sweeter than a typical empanada filling, then chill it until very firm (this prevents leaks).
Roll dough into rounds.
Place a spoonful of the cold, jellied filling along with egg, olives, and raisins onto each round.
Fold and crimp the edges into a distinctive braided seal.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until golden, about 20-25 minutes.

dishes.name: Asado Uruguayo
dishes.description: Uruguay's version of the South American barbecue tradition.
steps: Build a wood fire and let it burn down to steady embers.
Season the meat simply with coarse salt.
Grill slowly over indirect heat, turning occasionally, until deeply browned and cooked through.
Grill chorizo alongside until browned and cooked.
Rest briefly before serving with chimichurri or salad.

dishes.name: Chivito
dishes.description: Loaded Uruguayan steak sandwich piled with toppings.
steps: Season the thin beef steaks with salt and pepper. Preheat a grill or grill pan to medium-high heat.
Grill the steaks for 3-4 minutes per side (for medium), or until cooked to your preferred doneness.
During the last minute of cooking, lay a slice of ham and a slice of cheese on top of each steak, and cover the pan briefly (or close the grill lid) so the cheese melts slightly.
In a separate pan, fry the eggs sunny-side up until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny, about 2-3 minutes.
Lightly toast the bread rolls, cut-side down, in a dry pan or under the broiler for a minute or two until golden.

Build the sandwich: place the steak with melted cheese and ham on the toasted roll, top with the fried egg, and add lettuce, tomato, or other toppings as you like. Serve immediately while everything is hot.

dishes.name: Ropa Vieja
dishes.description: Cuba's national dish of slow-cooked shredded beef in tomato sauce.
steps: Place the flank steak in a large pot with a quartered onion, a bay leaf, a few peppercorns, and enough water to cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer, cover, and cook for 1.5-2 hours, until the meat is fork-tender and shreds easily.

Remove the beef from the pot and let it cool slightly, reserving about a cup of the cooking broth. Once cool enough to handle, shred the meat into thin strips using two forks, pulling it apart along the grain.
Heat oil in a large skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat. Sauté sliced onion and bell pepper for 6-8 minutes until softened and starting to caramelize at the edges.
Add minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant, then stir in cumin and a pinch of oregano.
Add the tomato sauce and the reserved cooking broth, stirring to combine, and bring to a simmer.

Add the shredded beef to the pan, stirring to coat it in the sauce. Simmer uncovered for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and clings to the meat and the flavors meld together.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt, pepper, and a splash of vinegar or lime juice for brightness if needed.
Serve hot over white rice with black beans on the side.

dishes.name: Moros y Cristianos
dishes.description: Cuban black beans and rice cooked together, named for their contrasting colors.
steps: If using dried black beans, soak them overnight, then cook in fresh water until tender, about 1-1.5 hours, and reserve the cooking liquid. If using canned beans, drain but reserve the liquid from the can.
In a large pot, heat oil and sauté diced onion, bell pepper, and garlic for 5-6 minutes until softened and fragrant.
Stir in cumin, oregano, and a bay leaf, cooking for 30 seconds to bloom the spices.
Add the rinsed rice to the pot and stir to coat it in the oil and aromatics for a minute or two.
Add the cooked black beans along with their reserved liquid, topping up with water or stock so the total liquid is about double the volume of the rice.
Bring to a boil, season with salt, then reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and cook undisturbed for 18-20 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from heat and let stand, covered, for 5 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork, mixing the beans evenly through the rice before serving.

dishes.name: Mangú
dishes.description: Mashed boiled plantains, a Dominican breakfast staple.
steps: Boil peeled green plantains in salted water until very soft.
Mash the hot plantains with a little of the cooking water and butter until smooth.
Sauté sliced onion in oil with a splash of vinegar until soft and tangy.
Spread the pickled onions over the mashed plantain.
Serve warm, often with fried cheese, eggs, and salami.

dishes.name: Sancocho
dishes.description: Hearty root vegetable and meat stew found in many Latin American countries, with regional variations.
steps: Simmer the mixed meats in a large pot of water with onion and garlic until tender.
Add yuca, corn, plantain, and other root vegetables.
Simmer until all the vegetables are tender and the broth is rich and flavorful, about an hour total.
Skim any excess fat from the surface.
Serve hot in deep bowls with rice on the side.

dishes.name: Pepián
dishes.description: Guatemala's national dish, a stew thickened with toasted spices and seeds.
steps: Toast sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, and dried chilies in a dry pan until fragrant.
Blend the toasted seeds and chilies with tomato into a smooth sauce.
Brown chicken pieces, then add the blended sauce and enough water to cover.
Add potato and simmer until the chicken and potato are tender, about 40 minutes.
Serve with rice.

dishes.name: Baleada
dishes.description: Simple, beloved Honduran folded tortilla with beans and cheese.
steps: Heat the flour tortillas on a dry griddle or skillet over medium heat, about 30-45 seconds per side, until warm, soft, and lightly speckled.
In a small saucepan, warm the refried beans over low heat, stirring and adding a splash of water if needed, until smooth and spreadable.
Spread a generous layer of the warm refried beans over one half of each warm tortilla, leaving a small border.
Sprinkle the crumbled queso fresco evenly over the beans, then drizzle with crema.
If adding scrambled egg or avocado, prepare and add them now, layering over the cheese.
Fold the tortilla in half over the filling, pressing gently, and serve warm immediately.

dishes.name: Gallo Pinto
dishes.description: Central American breakfast staple of rice and beans cooked together.
steps: Sauté onion and bell pepper until softened.
Add cooked black beans along with a little of their liquid.
Add the cooked rice, stirring to combine and coat the grains in the bean liquid.
Cook, stirring occasionally, until everything is well combined and slightly darker in color.
Serve for breakfast, often with eggs and plantain.

dishes.name: Casado
dishes.description: Costa Rican combination plate, literally 'married' rice, beans, and sides.
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it according to package directions, typically simmered covered with a 2:1 water-to-rice ratio until tender and fluffy, about 18-20 minutes.
Cook the black beans: if using canned, warm them in a pot with a little of their liquid, some diced onion, and garlic; if using dried, cook them ahead until fully tender in plenty of water.
Season and cook your protein of choice (chicken, beef, fish, or pork) — season with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lime, then pan-sear or grill until fully cooked and nicely browned on the outside.
Slice ripe plantains on a diagonal and fry in a little oil over medium heat for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and caramelized (ripe plantains cook much faster than green ones used for tostones).
Make a simple cabbage salad by tossing shredded cabbage with lime juice, a little oil, salt, and chopped tomato.
Arrange everything on a large plate in separate sections: a mound of rice, a scoop of beans, the cooked protein, fried plantains, and the cabbage salad, so each component stays distinct.
Serve with lime wedges and, if you like, a small dish of hot sauce on the side.

dishes.name: Griot
dishes.description: Haitian fried pork, marinated in citrus and served with spicy pickled slaw.
steps: Marinate pork cubes in sour orange juice, garlic, and scotch bonnet for at least 2 hours.
Simmer the pork in its marinade with a little water until tender, about 45 minutes.
Drain the pork, reserving the liquid.
Fry the tender pork pieces in hot oil until deeply browned and crispy outside.
Serve with pikliz and fried plantain.

dishes.name: Pikliz
dishes.description: Fiery Haitian pickled cabbage relish, served alongside fried dishes.
steps: Combine shredded cabbage, carrot, and scotch bonnet in a large jar.
Pack the vegetables tightly.
Pour white vinegar over the top until fully submerged.
Seal and let sit at room temperature for at least 24 hours before using.
Store refrigerated; it keeps for weeks and grows tangier over time.

dishes.name: Pastel de Choclo
dishes.description: Chilean corn pie layered over a savory beef filling.
steps: Cook ground beef with onion and warming spices for the filling.
Blend fresh corn with a little milk and sugar into a thick, slightly sweet puree.
Spread the beef filling with olives and egg pieces in the bottom of a baking dish.
Top with the corn puree in an even layer.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the top is golden, about 30-35 minutes.

dishes.name: Curanto
dishes.description: Traditional Chilote dish of seafood and meat slow-cooked underground.
steps: Dig a pit and build a hot fire with stones inside it, letting it burn down until the stones are extremely hot and glowing (this typically takes an hour or more) - alternatively, if you don't have access to an outdoor pit, this dish can be approximated in a very large covered pot with a steamer layer, though it won't be truly traditional.
Once the stones are hot, remove the burning wood, leaving the hot stones at the bottom of the pit.

Line the pit with large edible leaves (or aluminum foil as a substitute), then build up layers: a layer of shellfish, a layer of pork and chicken pieces, and a layer of potatoes, separating each layer with more large leaves so flavors and juices mingle without everything turning to mush.
Cover the entire pit tightly with more leaves, then with earth or a heavy tarp, to trap all the steam and heat inside.
Let it cook undisturbed for 1.5 to 2 hours - resist the urge to peek, since every time you open it, heat and steam escape and cooking time increases.
Carefully uncover the pit, lifting away the leaves in the order you added them, and serve everything together while hot, straight from the layers.

dishes.name: Empanada de Pino
dishes.description: Chile's baked empanada filled with spiced beef, olives, and egg.
steps: Cook ground beef slowly with a generous amount of diced onion until the onion nearly melts into the meat.
Let the filling cool completely.
Place filling with a slice of egg and an olive onto each pastry disc.
Fold into a half-moon and crimp the edges into a decorative seal.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until golden, about 25-30 minutes.

dishes.name: Doubles
dishes.description: Trinidad's beloved street food of curried chickpeas sandwiched in fried bread.
steps: Make a soft, turmeric-tinted yeasted dough and let it rise.
Flatten small portions into thin rounds and fry briefly until puffed (these are the 'bara').
Prepare a curried chickpea filling, seasoned with curry powder and pepper.
Sandwich a spoonful of curried chickpeas between two bara.
Serve with tamarind and pepper sauces.

dishes.name: Trinidadian Roti
dishes.description: Soft flatbread wrapped around curry, reflecting Trinidad's Indian heritage.
steps: Make a soft dough from flour, water, and a little ghee, then rest it.
Roll into large thin rounds and griddle, brushing with ghee, until cooked through and flaky.
Prepare a curry filling of choice.
Spoon the curry into the center of the roti.
Fold the roti around the filling like a parcel and serve warm.

dishes.name: Cou-Cou and Flying Fish
dishes.description: Barbados' national dish pairing a cornmeal-okra mash with steamed fish.
steps: Simmer sliced okra in water until soft.
Gradually whisk in cornmeal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps, until it forms a thick, smooth mash.
Season fish with lime and spices, then steam or poach until just cooked through.
Shape the cou-cou into a mound.
Serve alongside the steamed fish and a light gravy.

dishes.name: Ackee and Saltfish
dishes.description: Jamaica's national dish, combining a unique local fruit with salted fish.
steps: Place the salted cod in a bowl, cover generously with cold water, and refrigerate. Soak for several hours or overnight, changing the water 2-3 times, to draw out the excess salt.

Drain the cod, place it in a pot of fresh water, and simmer for about 15-20 minutes until tender. Drain, let cool slightly, then flake the fish into bite-sized pieces with a fork, discarding any skin or bones.

Heat a little oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the diced onion, diced tomato, and thinly sliced scotch bonnet pepper (use gloves and avoid touching your face when handling it - it's extremely hot), and cook for 5-6 minutes until softened.
Add the flaked saltfish to the pan and cook for 3-4 minutes, stirring, to heat through and let the flavors combine.
Gently add the canned ackee on top, folding it into the mixture very carefully with a spatula - ackee is delicate and breaks apart easily, so use a light touch, more folding than stirring.
Warm everything through for 2-3 minutes without stirring too much, then serve hot with fried dumplings or breadfruit.

dishes.name: Curry Goat
dishes.description: Jamaican slow-cooked curried goat, a centerpiece of celebrations.
steps: Cut goat meat into large chunks, leaving some bone in if possible for extra flavor.
Marinate the goat in curry powder, garlic, thyme, and a little scotch bonnet for at least a few hours, ideally overnight.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and brown the marinated goat on all sides.
Add diced onion and cook until softened.
Add enough water to mostly cover the meat, bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer.
Cover and simmer gently for 1.5-2 hours, checking occasionally — goat needs this long, slow cooking to become tender.
About 30 minutes before the end, add potato chunks and cook until soft in the sauce.
Taste and adjust seasoning, adding more scotch bonnet for heat if you like.
Serve hot over rice, with the meat falling easily off the bone.

dishes.name: Jambalaya
dishes.description: Louisiana Creole rice dish loaded with meat and the holy trinity of vegetables.
steps: Dice the onion, celery, and bell pepper into small, even pieces — this trio, known as 'the trinity' in Cajun cooking, is the flavor foundation, similar to how mirepoix works in French cooking.
In a large, heavy pot, brown sliced andouille sausage over medium-high heat until it develops some color, then remove and set aside.
In the same pot (leaving the flavorful fat behind), sauté the trinity of vegetables until softened, about 5-6 minutes.
Add minced garlic and Cajun seasoning, cooking for another minute until fragrant.
Add rice to the pot and stir well, letting it toast slightly in the fat and vegetables for a minute or two — this adds flavor and helps the grains cook up more distinct rather than mushy.
Return the browned sausage to the pot, along with diced chicken if using.
Pour in chicken stock and diced tomatoes, stirring once to combine, then bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and let it simmer undisturbed for about 20 minutes — resist stirring during this time, since it disrupts the rice's cooking.

In the last 5 minutes, add shrimp on top of the rice (don't stir them in yet), cover again, and let the residual heat and steam finish cooking them through — shrimp overcook fast, so this timing matters.
Once the rice is tender and the shrimp are pink and just cooked, gently fold everything together with a fork.
Taste and adjust seasoning — Cajun seasoning blends vary a lot in saltiness, so this is the moment to fine-tune.
Serve hot, garnished with sliced scallion if you like.

dishes.name: Lobster Roll
dishes.description: Chilled or buttered lobster meat served in a toasted split-top bun.
steps: Steam or boil lobster until just cooked through, then cool and chop the meat.
Toss the lobster meat lightly with mayonnaise (or melted butter for a warm version), keeping it chunky.
Season with a squeeze of lemon and a little celery for crunch, if desired.
Toast a split-top hot dog bun with butter until golden.
Pile the lobster salad into the toasted bun and serve immediately.

dishes.name: Philly Cheesesteak
dishes.description: Philadelphia's iconic sandwich of griddled beef and cheese.
steps: Thinly slice ribeye or use pre-shaved beef.
Griddle the beef with sliced onion until cooked through, chopping it into smaller pieces as it cooks.
Melt cheese (traditionally Cheez Whiz or provolone) directly over the meat on the griddle.
Scoop the meat and melted cheese into a long hoagie roll.
Serve hot, with or without peppers.

dishes.name: Chicago Deep Dish Pizza
dishes.description: Pizza baked in a deep pan with cheese under a chunky tomato sauce.
steps: Press thick dough into a deep, well-oiled pan, pushing it up the sides.
Layer sliced mozzarella directly onto the dough.
Add cooked crumbled sausage over the cheese.
Pour crushed tomato sauce over the top (sauce goes on last in Chicago style).
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 30-35 minutes until the crust is golden and cooked through.

dishes.name: Fajitas
dishes.description: Sizzling grilled meat and pepper strips wrapped in warm tortillas.
steps: Marinate the meat in lime juice, garlic, and spices for at least 30 minutes.
Grill or sear the meat until charred outside and cooked to preference, then slice.
Sauté bell pepper and onion until slightly charred but still crisp.
Warm the tortillas.
Serve the sliced meat and vegetables sizzling hot with warm tortillas and toppings.

dishes.name: Texas Brisket
dishes.description: Slow-smoked beef brisket, the centerpiece of Texas barbecue.
steps: Coat the brisket generously with dry rub.
Smoke at a low, steady temperature (225-250°F/107-121°C) for 10-14 hours until it reaches a tender internal texture.
Wrap in butcher paper partway through smoking to help retain moisture.
Rest the brisket for at least 30 minutes before slicing.
Slice against the grain and serve.

dishes.name: Shrimp and Grits
dishes.description: Creamy corn grits topped with seasoned shrimp, a Southern breakfast classic.
steps: Bring water or stock to a boil, then whisk in grits gradually.
Simmer, stirring often, until thick and creamy, about 20-25 minutes.
Stir in butter and cheese until melted and smooth.
Sauté seasoned shrimp in a separate pan until just pink.
Spoon shrimp and their pan sauce over the hot grits to serve.

dishes.name: Butter Tart
dishes.description: Small, gooey Canadian pastry tart with a caramel-like filling.
steps: Line small tart tins with pastry dough.
Melt butter and whisk with brown sugar and eggs until smooth.
Add a few raisins to the bottom of each tart shell if using.
Pour the filling into the shells, filling about two-thirds full.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15-18 minutes until the filling is just set with a slight jiggle in the center.

dishes.name: Tourtière
dishes.description: Québécois meat pie traditionally served during the winter holidays.
steps: Cook ground pork with onion and warming spices until browned.
Stir in mashed potato to bind and thicken the filling.
Let the filling cool, then spoon into a pastry-lined pie dish.
Top with the second pastry disc, sealing and venting the top.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for about 45 minutes until deeply golden.

dishes.name: Plov
dishes.description: Uzbekistan's national rice pilaf, cooked with lamb and carrots in one pot.
steps: Brown lamb cubes with onion in a heavy pot.
Add julienned carrot and cook until softened.
Stir in cumin and a little water, simmering until the lamb is nearly tender.
Add rice on top without stirring, then add enough water to just cover.
Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is tender, about 25 minutes, then fluff everything together.

dishes.name: Manti
dishes.description: Steamed dumplings found across Central Asia and Turkey, served with yogurt.
steps: Make a firm dough from flour and water, then rest it.
Mix ground meat with minced onion and seasoning.
Roll dough very thin and cut into small squares.
Place a small amount of filling in each square and pinch the corners together tightly.
Steam or boil until cooked through, then serve topped with yogurt-garlic sauce and a drizzle of paprika butter.

dishes.name: Lagman
dishes.description: Hand-pulled noodle dish with a spiced meat and vegetable topping.
steps: Stir-fry sliced meat until browned.
Add garlic, bell pepper, and tomato, cooking until softened into a light sauce.
Add a splash of stock and simmer briefly to bring the sauce together.
Cook hand-pulled (or substitute wide) noodles separately until tender.
Top the noodles generously with the meat and vegetable sauce.

dishes.name: Beshbarmak
dishes.description: Central Asian dish of boiled meat over noodles, traditionally eaten by hand.
steps: Simmer meat in water with onion until very tender, reserving the broth.
Cook flat pasta squares in the broth until tender.
Slice or shred the cooked meat.
Toss the noodles with some broth and top with sliced onion cooked briefly in the broth.
Arrange the meat over the noodles and serve with a cup of the hot broth on the side.

dishes.name: Khachapuri
dishes.description: Georgian cheese-filled bread, the boat-shaped version topped with a raw egg.
steps: Make a soft, enriched yeasted dough: dissolve yeast in warm milk with a little sugar, let it foam for 5-10 minutes, then mix with flour, salt, and a little oil into a soft dough. Knead for about 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Let the dough rise in a warm spot for about an hour, until roughly doubled in size.
Punch down the dough and divide it into portions. Roll each portion into an oval shape on a floured surface.
Mix your cheese filling — traditionally a combination of a few different cheeses, like mozzarella and feta, for a balance of meltiness and tang.
Spread the cheese filling down the center of each oval, leaving a border around the edges.

Roll the long edges of the dough up and over toward the center, pinching the ends together tightly to form a boat shape with the cheese visible down the middle — this takes a little practice, but even a rougher version will still taste great.
Let the shaped khachapuri rest for about 15 minutes to puff slightly before baking.
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for about 15-18 minutes, until the crust is golden and the cheese is melted and bubbling.
Remove from the oven and immediately crack a raw egg into the center of each one — the residual heat will gently cook the egg over the next couple of minutes without fully hardening it.

Add a small pat of butter to each and serve right away: the traditional way to eat khachapuri is to swirl the egg and butter into the melted cheese with a piece of the bread crust before tearing off pieces to eat.

dishes.name: Khinkali
dishes.description: Georgian soup dumplings, twisted at the top and held by the knot while eaten.
steps: Make a firm dough from flour and water, kneading until smooth, then rest it covered for at least 30 minutes.
Mix ground meat with minced onion, adding a splash of water or broth to the filling — this extra liquid becomes the flavorful broth inside each dumpling.
Roll the rested dough thin and cut into rounds, larger than typical dumpling wrappers, since khinkali need extra dough for the twisted top.
Place a generous spoonful of the juicy filling in the center of each round.
Gather the edges up and around the filling, pleating as you go around the circumference, then twist the gathered top tightly to seal, leaving a small knob at the top.
Boil the khinkali in salted water until they float and the dough is fully cooked, about 8-10 minutes.
Remove with a slotted spoon, draining excess water.
Serve hot, dusted generously with black pepper. Hold the topknot, bite from the side to release the hot broth inside and sip it, then eat the rest — leaving the tough topknot itself uneaten.

dishes.name: Lobio
dishes.description: Georgian spiced bean stew, often flavored with walnuts and coriander.
steps: Sauté onion and garlic until soft.
Mash a portion of the cooked beans and combine with the whole beans for a mixed texture.
Stir in ground walnuts and sautéed onion.
Simmer briefly to combine flavors, adding a little bean cooking liquid if needed.
Finish with fresh cilantro and a drizzle of walnut oil.

dishes.name: Armenian Dolma
dishes.description: Stuffed grape leaves or vegetables, a staple across the Caucasus and Armenian diaspora.
steps: Mix rice with ground lamb, minced onion, and chopped herbs.
Place a spoonful of filling on each grape leaf and roll tightly, tucking in the sides.
Layer the rolls snugly in a pot.
Add water or broth to just cover, weigh down with a plate, and simmer gently for about an hour.
Serve warm or at room temperature with yogurt.

dishes.name: Lavash
dishes.description: Thin, soft flatbread central to Armenian cuisine, baked in a clay oven.
steps: Mix flour, water, and salt into a firm, smooth dough, then rest it covered for 30 minutes.
Divide into small balls and roll each out very thin.
Cook on a very hot dry griddle or in a traditional clay oven (tandir) until lightly browned with a few char spots.
Stack the finished lavash and cover with a cloth to keep it soft.
Serve fresh alongside cheese, herbs, or grilled meats.

dishes.name: Masala Chai
dishes.description: Spiced milk tea, brewed strong and simmered with warming spices.
steps: In a saucepan, combine the water and lightly crushed spices (cardamom pods, a piece of ginger, cinnamon stick, cloves — crush the cardamom and smash the ginger to release their oils).
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and let the spices simmer for 5 minutes to build a strong, fragrant base.
Add the black tea (loose leaf or tea bags) and simmer for another 2-3 minutes until the water turns a deep reddish-brown.
Pour in the milk and bring the mixture back to a gentle boil, watching closely since milk can boil over quickly — reduce heat as soon as it starts to rise.
Let it simmer gently for 2-3 minutes so the tea, spices, and milk fully meld together.
Stir in sugar to taste, then strain the chai through a fine sieve directly into cups, pressing on the solids to extract every bit of flavor.
Serve hot immediately.

dishes.name: Lassi
dishes.description: Chilled yogurt drink, served sweet, salty, or fruit-flavored.
steps: In a blender or a large bowl, combine 2 cups plain yogurt and 1 cup water or milk.
Whisk (or blend on low) until completely smooth, with no lumps of yogurt remaining.
For a sweet lassi, add 3 tablespoons sugar and, if using, 1/4 teaspoon ground cardamom. For a savory lassi instead, use salt and a pinch of roasted, ground cumin in place of the sugar and cardamom.
Blend or whisk again for about 30 seconds, until the mixture looks light and slightly frothy on top.
Taste and adjust sweetness, saltiness, or thickness (add a splash more water or milk if it's too thick).
Chill in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes, then pour over ice to serve, garnishing with a pinch of cardamom or chopped nuts if desired.

dishes.name: Bubble Tea
dishes.description: Taiwanese tea drink with chewy tapioca pearls, now a global phenomenon.
steps: Boil tapioca pearls according to package directions until soft and chewy, then soak in sugar syrup.
Brew strong black tea and let it cool slightly.
Combine tea, milk, and sweetener, stirring well.
Add a scoop of tapioca pearls to the bottom of each glass.
Pour the milk tea over the pearls and serve with a wide straw.

dishes.name: Caipirinha
dishes.description: Brazil's national cocktail, muddled lime and sugar cane spirit.
steps: Cut the lime into quarters (leave the peel on).
Place the lime quarters in the bottom of a sturdy, short glass along with 2 teaspoons sugar.
